units.title: Energy in Chemical Reactions
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A disposable hand warmer heats up when you open the package and expose it to air, but an instant cold pack gets cold when you squeeze it and break the inner pouch. Both involve chemical reactions — why does one release heat while the other absorbs it?
essential_questions: How can we measure and predict the energy changes that occur during chemical reactions?
What role does bond breaking and bond forming play in determining whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic?
How do potential energy diagrams help us visualize the energy changes in a reaction?
units.crse_theme: Students examine how energy transformations in chemical reactions connect to cultural practices and real-world applications, including traditional metallurgy in West Africa (iron smelting requiring understanding of exothermic reactions), the chemistry of cooking across cultures, and the environmental justice implications of industrial energy use in communities of color.

formative: Exit tickets on exothermic vs. endothermic classification
summative: Unit 6 Exam: Energy in Chemical Reactions

investigations: Investigation 6: Calorimetry — Measuring the Heat of Dissolution

lessons.title: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify a chemical reaction as exothermic or endothermic based on temperature change data and explain the direction of energy flow between the system and surroundings.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is the hottest or coldest thing you have ever touched? What happened to your body when you touched it?
lessons.do_now: A student mixes baking soda and vinegar in a beaker. The temperature drops 5 degrees C. Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic? How do you know?
materials: Thermometers or temperature probes (1 per group)
Commercial hand warmer and cold pack (1 each for demo)

engage.description: Pass around an activated hand warmer and an activated cold pack. Students touch both and record the temperature sensation. Ask: Both involve chemicals reacting — why does one feel hot and the other cold? Where is the energy coming from or going to? Students write initial hypotheses in notebooks.

explore.description: In pairs, students conduct two mini-experiments. Experiment A: Dissolve calcium chloride in water and record the temperature change every 30 seconds for 3 minutes. Experiment B: Dissolve ammonium nitrate in water and record temperature changes on the same schedule. Students graph both data sets on the same axes using different colors.

explain.description: Teacher defines system (the chemicals reacting) and surroundings (everything else, including the water and cup). In exothermic reactions, energy flows from system to surroundings, so surroundings get warmer. In endothermic reactions, energy flows from surroundings to system, so surroundings get cooler. Students label their graphs and complete an energy flow diagram showing arrows for each reaction type.

elaborate.description: Students classify five real-world processes as exothermic or endothermic: combustion of gasoline, photosynthesis, cooking an egg, ice melting, and rusting of iron. For each, they identify the system and surroundings and draw the energy flow arrow.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A student dissolves a mystery salt in water and the temperature rises from 22 degrees C to 35 degrees C. (1) Is this process exothermic or endothermic? (2) Did the system release or absorb energy? (3) Draw an energy flow diagram with labeled arrows.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-drawn energy flow diagram template with labeled boxes for system and surroundings; include sentence starters for classifying reactions: 'This reaction is ___ because the temperature of the surroundings ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the two dissolution experiments and classification activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain why ammonium nitrate cold packs are used in first aid instead of ice, and calculate which provides more cooling per gram using provided enthalpy data.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with visual energy flow diagrams labeled in English and Spanish; use color-coding (red for exothermic, blue for endothermic) consistently throughout materials.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted data table with time intervals already filled in; partner with a peer for temperature readings; reduce classification problems from five to three.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of traditional cooking methods across cultures — tandoori ovens (sustained exothermic combustion), Korean ondol floor heating (using combustion heat transfer), and the endothermic process of evaporative cooling used in Nigerian clay pot refrigerators (zeer pots). Highlight how communities engineered energy solutions long before formal thermochemistry.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'exothermic reaction': The hand warmer feels hot because___. Both the hand warmer and the cold pack involve chemical reactions, but___. The temperature of the surroundings increased, so we know the reaction is___.

vocabulary.definition: A process that releases energy to the surroundings, usually observed as an increase in temperature
A process that absorbs energy from the surroundings, usually observed as a decrease in temperature
The specific part of the universe being studied, typically the reactants and products in a chemical reaction
Everything outside the system that can exchange energy with it
The transfer of thermal energy between objects at different temperatures
The total heat content of a system; changes in enthalpy measure heat absorbed or released at constant pressure

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: System vs. Surroundings — Defining the Boundary
Section 2: Exothermic Reactions — Energy Released to Surroundings
Section 3: Endothermic Reactions — Energy Absorbed from Surroundings
Section 4: Classifying Reactions Using Temperature Data

cer.phenomenon: A camping supply company sells two products: a hand warmer that uses iron powder exposed to air, and a cold pack that contains ammonium nitrate and water separated by a thin membrane. When you squeeze the cold pack, the membrane breaks and the pack gets very cold.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the hand warmer undergoes a(n) ___ reaction and the cold pack undergoes a(n) ___ reaction because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use temperature data from the dissolution experiments and energy flow diagrams to support your classification of each product.
cer.reasoning_frame: The hand warmer releases energy to the surroundings because___. This is consistent with a(n) ___ reaction where the energy of the products is ___ than the energy of the reactants. The cold pack, however,___ because___.

lessons.title: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can draw and interpret a potential energy diagram for exothermic and endothermic reactions, labeling reactants, products, activation energy, and enthalpy change.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of something that needed a push to get started but then kept going on its own — like pushing a car downhill. What was the initial push?
lessons.do_now: A match will not light on its own, but once you strike it, it burns completely. Why does the match need that initial strike if burning releases energy?
materials: Potential energy diagram template (printed, 2 per student)
PE diagram card sorting activity (set of 12 cards per group)
PhET simulation: 'Reactions & Rates' (projected or on devices)

engage.description: Analogy: Show an image of a person pushing a boulder up and over a hill. On the other side, the boulder rolls down to a lower elevation. Ask: The boulder ends up lower than where it started — it lost energy overall. But it needed energy to get over the hill first. How is this like a chemical reaction? Students sketch the hill analogy and label it.

explore.description: Card sorting: Each group receives 12 cards showing PE diagrams with various features (high activation energy, low activation energy, large exothermic change, small endothermic change, with and without catalysts). Students sort them into categories and identify patterns. Then using the PhET Reactions & Rates simulation, students adjust activation energy and observe how it affects whether reactions proceed.

explain.description: Teacher builds a labeled PE diagram step-by-step on the board. Key features: (1) reactant energy level, (2) activated complex at the peak, (3) product energy level, (4) activation energy (Ea) as the difference between reactants and the peak, (5) enthalpy change (delta H) as the difference between reactants and products. Students draw both an exothermic diagram (products lower) and endothermic diagram (products higher) with all labels.

elaborate.description: Students receive a PE diagram showing a reaction with and without a catalyst. They identify how the catalyst changes the diagram (lowers the activation energy peak but does not change delta H). Then they answer: A catalyst speeds up a reaction. Using the diagram, explain why lowering Ea makes the reaction faster. Connect to real-world catalysts: catalytic converters in cars, enzymes in digestion.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given numerical values (reactant PE = 80 kJ, product PE = 30 kJ, activation energy = 60 kJ), students (1) draw a labeled PE diagram, (2) calculate delta H, (3) classify the reaction as exothermic or endothermic, (4) determine the PE of the activated complex.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a PE diagram template with axes pre-labeled and dotted lines showing where to draw reactant and product energy levels; include a step-by-step checklist for labeling each feature.
differentiation.on_level: Complete PE diagram construction and interpretation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given a PE diagram for a reversible reaction, students draw the PE diagram for the reverse reaction and compare the activation energies and delta H values for forward and reverse directions.
differentiation.ell: Color-coded PE diagram with a bilingual key (activation energy in red, delta H in blue, labels in English and native language); sentence frames for describing energy changes.
differentiation.iep: Enlarged PE diagram templates; reduce the exit ticket to two parts instead of four; allow use of reference card showing labeled sample diagrams.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the role of catalysts in industrial chemistry and connect to the work of Elinor Ostrom on managing common resources, and the contributions of Gertrude Elion, a Nobel Prize-winning biochemist whose work on enzyme inhibitors (which function by altering activation energy pathways) led to drugs treating leukemia, herpes, and organ transplant rejection. She was initially denied lab positions because of gender discrimination.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'Activation energy, the minimum energy required for reactants to form the activated complex and begin reacting, determines how easily a reaction starts.' 'A catalyst, a substance that lowers the activation energy without being consumed in the reaction, increases the reaction rate without changing the overall energy change.'

vocabulary.definition: A graph that shows the energy changes that occur during a chemical reaction, with the reaction pathway on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis
The minimum amount of energy required for reactants to reach the activated complex and begin reacting
A temporary, high-energy, unstable arrangement of atoms that forms at the peak of the potential energy diagram during the transition from reactants to products
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by lowering the activation energy without being consumed or permanently changed
The difference in heat content between products and reactants; negative for exothermic reactions, positive for endothermic reactions

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is a Potential Energy Diagram?
Section 2: Reading the Diagram — Reactants, Products, Activated Complex
Section 3: Activation Energy — The Energy Barrier
Section 4: Exothermic vs. Endothermic PE Diagrams
Section 5: How Catalysts Change the Diagram

cer.phenomenon: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) decomposes very slowly at room temperature into water and oxygen gas. When a small amount of manganese dioxide (MnO2) is added, the decomposition happens rapidly with visible bubbling, but the MnO2 can be recovered unchanged after the reaction.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that manganese dioxide acts as a ___ in this reaction because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use evidence from the PE diagram card sort and the definition of a catalyst to explain how MnO2 affects the energy profile of the decomposition reaction.
cer.reasoning_frame: The MnO2 ___ the activation energy of the decomposition reaction, which means___. The fact that MnO2 can be recovered unchanged confirms it is a ___ because___. The overall enthalpy change (delta H) ___ because___.

lessons.title: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can use the equation q = mCdeltaT to calculate the heat absorbed or released during a physical or chemical change and interpret the sign of q.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is a food or drink that you eat at a specific temperature — really hot or really cold? Why does the temperature matter for that food?
lessons.do_now: You heat 100 grams of water and 100 grams of iron to the same temperature and then let them cool. Which one cools faster? Why might different materials lose heat at different rates?
materials: Thermometers or digital temperature probes (1 per group)
Metal samples: aluminum, copper, iron (pre-heated in hot water bath)

engage.description: Scenario: A lifeguard walks barefoot across a concrete pool deck and then steps onto a metal diving board. Both surfaces are in the same sunlight at the same air temperature. The metal feels much hotter. Ask: If they are at the same temperature, why does the metal feel hotter? Introduce the idea that different materials transfer heat at different rates, which connects to specific heat capacity.

explore.description: Calorimetry lab: Each group receives a pre-heated metal sample (identity unknown). They measure the mass of the metal and the mass and initial temperature of water in their calorimeter. They add the hot metal to the cool water, stir gently, and record the final equilibrium temperature. Groups then use q = mCdeltaT to calculate the heat gained by the water and, assuming no heat loss, set this equal to the heat lost by the metal to solve for the specific heat capacity of the unknown metal.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the calorimetry equation: q = mCdeltaT, where q is heat in joules, m is mass in grams, C is specific heat capacity in J/g degrees C, and deltaT is the change in temperature. Key points: positive q means heat is absorbed, negative q means heat is released. In a calorimeter, q(water) = -q(metal). Students compare their calculated specific heat values to a reference table to identify their unknown metal.

elaborate.description: Practice problems: (1) How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 250 g of water from 20 degrees C to 80 degrees C? (2) A 50 g piece of copper (C = 0.385 J/g degrees C) cools from 95 degrees C to 25 degrees C. How much heat did it release? (3) If 5000 J of heat is added to 200 g of an unknown substance and the temperature rises by 12.5 degrees C, what is the specific heat capacity?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A student heats 150 g of water in a calorimeter from 22.0 degrees C to 34.5 degrees C by dissolving a salt. (1) Calculate the heat absorbed by the water (C of water = 4.18 J/g degrees C). (2) Was the dissolution exothermic or endothermic? Explain using the sign of q for the salt.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a calorimetry calculation template with the formula written out and blanks for each variable; include a worked example alongside each practice problem.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the calorimetry lab and calculation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the percent error between experimental specific heat and accepted value; analyze sources of heat loss in the calorimeter and propose design improvements.
differentiation.ell: Provide a formula card with variable definitions in English and native language; use color-coding to match variables in the equation to their positions in the data table.
differentiation.iep: Allow calculator use for all problems; provide pre-organized data tables; reduce practice problems to two; allow extended time on lab calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight the work of Wilbur Scoville, who developed the Scoville scale for measuring pepper heat using dilution methods, and connect to the chemistry of capsaicin. Discuss how communities in Mexico, India, and West Africa cultivated hot peppers for millennia — the sensation of heat from capsaicin is a chemical interaction with nerve receptors, not an actual temperature change, contrasting perceived heat with measurable heat (q).
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'specific heat capacity': Water has a high specific heat capacity because___. Metals feel hotter in the sun than wood at the same temperature, but their actual temperatures are the same, so___. The specific heat capacity of a substance is large, so it takes ___ energy to change its temperature.

vocabulary.definition: The measurement of heat changes during chemical or physical processes using a device called a calorimeter
The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 degree Celsius
The energy transferred between objects due to a temperature difference, measured in joules
The SI unit of energy; 4.18 joules equals 1 calorie
The difference between final and initial temperature, calculated as T(final) minus T(initial)
An insulated device used to measure the heat absorbed or released during a reaction or physical change

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is Calorimetry? — Measuring Heat Changes
Section 2: The Calorimetry Equation: q = mCdeltaT
Section 3: Specific Heat Capacity — Why Different Materials Heat Differently
Section 4: Solving Calorimetry Problems Step by Step
Section 5: Interpreting the Sign of q — Exothermic vs. Endothermic

cer.phenomenon: Two students each dissolve a different salt in 100 g of water at 22 degrees C. Student A's solution reaches 35 degrees C. Student B's solution drops to 15 degrees C. Both used the same mass of salt (10 g).
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Student A's salt underwent a(n) ___ dissolution and Student B's salt underwent a(n) ___ dissolution because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate q for each student's experiment using q = mCdeltaT and use the sign of q to classify each process.
cer.reasoning_frame: Student A's water temperature ___, meaning the water ___ heat from the dissolving salt. Therefore q for the water is ___ and q for the salt is ___, which means the dissolution is ___. Student B's water temperature ___, so___.

lessons.title: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how breaking bonds requires energy and forming bonds releases energy, and use bond energy data to determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about building something and then taking it apart — like a LEGO set or a puzzle. Which takes more effort: putting it together or breaking it apart?
lessons.do_now: In the reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, bonds in H2 and Cl2 must break before new H-Cl bonds can form. If breaking bonds requires energy, where does the energy come from to start the reaction?
materials: Bond energy data table (printed, 1 per student)
Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
Colored pencils (red for energy absorbed, green for energy released)

engage.description: Molecular model demo: Build H2 and Cl2 molecules using model kits in front of class. Physically pull them apart (break bonds) and say: 'This required energy — I had to do work.' Then connect the atoms into 2 HCl molecules and say: 'Forming new bonds releases energy.' Ask: If the energy released by forming H-Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl bonds, what happens to the extra energy?

explore.description: Using bond energy tables, students work in groups to calculate the total energy required to break all bonds in the reactants and the total energy released by forming all bonds in the products for three reactions: (1) H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, (2) N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, (3) CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. For each, they determine whether the net energy change is positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: delta H = (energy to break bonds in reactants) - (energy released forming bonds in products). If more energy is released than absorbed, delta H is negative (exothermic). If more energy is absorbed than released, delta H is positive (endothermic). Students create energy bar charts showing energy in vs. energy out for each of their three reactions.

elaborate.description: Application: Students examine why combustion reactions (burning fuels) are always exothermic. They compare bond energies in hydrocarbons (C-H and C-C bonds broken) with the very strong bonds formed (C=O in CO2 and O-H in H2O). The strong product bonds release more energy than is needed to break the weaker reactant bonds.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given bond energies (H-H = 436 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, O-H = 463 kJ/mol), calculate delta H for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Show all work and classify the reaction.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a bond-counting organizer that walks students through each molecule step by step: 'In H2, how many H-H bonds? ___ x ___ kJ = ___ kJ total.' Include a completed example for the first reaction.
differentiation.on_level: Complete bond energy calculations and energy bar charts as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Compare bond energy estimates of delta H to actual experimental delta H values from a reference table and explain why they differ (bond energies are averages, real bonds vary with molecular environment).
differentiation.ell: Provide bond energy vocabulary card with visual diagrams showing bonds breaking (with a '+' energy arrow) and forming (with a '-' energy arrow); sentence frames for explaining calculations.
differentiation.iep: Pre-counted bond inventory for each reaction; reduced number of reactions from three to two; allow partner work for calculations; enlarged bond energy table.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the work of Marie Maynard Daly, the first African American woman to earn a PhD in chemistry (1947, Columbia University). Her research on cholesterol metabolism and the biochemistry of heart attacks involved understanding how bond energies in biological molecules relate to metabolic energy. Also connect to how Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest used controlled burns (exothermic combustion) for land management, demonstrating intuitive understanding of energy release in reactions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'bond energy': Breaking bonds in the reactants requires energy because___. The reaction releases heat overall, but energy was still needed to break bonds first, so___. The bonds in the products are stronger than the bonds in the reactants, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in a gaseous molecule, measured in kJ/mol
An endothermic process that requires energy input to separate bonded atoms
An exothermic process that releases energy when new bonds are created between atoms
The net energy change in a reaction, equal to energy absorbed by bond breaking minus energy released by bond forming
A rapid exothermic reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen to produce heat and light

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Bond Breaking — An Endothermic Process
Section 2: Bond Forming — An Exothermic Process
Section 3: Calculating Delta H Using Bond Energies
Section 4: Energy Bar Charts — Visualizing Energy In vs. Energy Out
Section 5: Why Combustion Reactions Are Always Exothermic

cer.phenomenon: Natural gas (methane, CH4) is burned in home furnaces to heat houses in winter. The reaction CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O releases 890 kJ per mole of methane. A classmate says 'burning methane doesn't require any energy input because it releases energy.'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the classmate's statement is incorrect because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use bond energy data to show that energy is required to break C-H and O=O bonds before the exothermic bond-forming step can occur.
cer.reasoning_frame: Even though combustion is exothermic overall, the reaction requires ___ to break the ___ bonds in the reactants. This is the activation energy. The reaction is exothermic because the energy released by forming ___ bonds in the products is ___ than the energy required to break reactant bonds, resulting in a net release of ___ kJ.

lessons.title: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply Hess's Law to calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction by combining two or more thermochemical equations.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever taken a detour to get somewhere? Did the total distance change depending on the path you took, or was something about the trip the same regardless?
lessons.do_now: The direct flight from New York to Los Angeles is about 3,950 km. If you fly from New York to Chicago (1,150 km) and then Chicago to Los Angeles (2,800 km), the total is 3,950 km. What pattern do you notice? How might this relate to energy in chemical reactions?
materials: Thermochemical equation cards (set of 8 per group for puzzle activity)

engage.description: Elevation analogy: Show a diagram of a hiker going from point A (sea level) to point B (mountaintop, 2000 m). Path 1 is direct; Path 2 goes through an intermediate valley and then up. Ask: Does the overall elevation change depend on the path? No — it only depends on the starting and ending points. Introduce Hess's Law: the total enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not the pathway.

explore.description: Puzzle activity: Groups receive thermochemical equation cards and a target reaction. They must arrange and combine the given equations (reversing or multiplying as needed) so they add up to the target reaction. When equations are combined, their delta H values are added. Groups work through two puzzles of increasing difficulty on their whiteboards.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the rules of Hess's Law: (1) If a reaction is reversed, the sign of delta H is reversed. (2) If a reaction is multiplied by a coefficient, delta H is multiplied by the same coefficient. (3) When reactions are added, their delta H values are added. Walk through a complete worked example: Calculate delta H for C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO(g) using the given reactions for C -> CO2 and CO -> CO2.

elaborate.description: Students solve two additional Hess's Law problems independently. Problem 1: Calculate delta H for the formation of nitrogen dioxide from nitrogen and oxygen using two step reactions. Problem 2: Use three given thermochemical equations to find delta H for the combustion of ethanol.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given two thermochemical equations — (1) S(s) + O2(g) -> SO2(g), delta H = -297 kJ and (2) 2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g), delta H = -198 kJ — calculate delta H for S(s) + 3/2 O2(g) -> SO3(g). Show all steps.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step Hess's Law procedure card: Step 1 — Identify the target reaction. Step 2 — Check if each given reaction needs to be reversed. Step 3 — Check if coefficients need adjusting. Step 4 — Add equations and delta H values. Include a fully worked example alongside.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the puzzle activity and practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Apply Hess's Law to calculate the enthalpy of formation of glucose (C6H12O6) from combustion data and compare to the energy stored in food, calculating how many grams of glucose provide 2000 Calories.
differentiation.ell: Provide thermochemical equation cards with visual molecule diagrams alongside chemical formulas; use color-coded arrows for reversed reactions; bilingual procedure card.
differentiation.iep: Reduce puzzle complexity to single reversal or single multiplication; provide completed first step for each practice problem; allow partner work; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Germain Hess, a Swiss-Russian chemist who formulated Hess's Law in 1840, and the broader international nature of thermochemistry. Connect to modern applications: Hess's Law is used in food science to calculate the caloric content of complex meals. Explore how different cultural diets (Mediterranean, Japanese, West African) are analyzed using calorimetry and enthalpy calculations for nutritional science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Hess's Law': Hess's Law states that enthalpy change is independent of pathway because___. We cannot directly measure the enthalpy change of some reactions, but we can use Hess's Law, so___. The reaction was reversed, so the sign of delta H was___.

vocabulary.definition: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of whether the reaction occurs in one step or multiple steps
A balanced chemical equation that includes the enthalpy change (delta H) for the reaction
A property that depends only on the current state of a system, not on the path taken to reach that state; enthalpy is a state function
The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Hess's Law — Enthalpy is Path-Independent
Section 2: Rules for Manipulating Thermochemical Equations
Section 3: Step-by-Step Method for Solving Hess's Law Problems
Section 4: Practice — Combining Equations to Find Delta H

cer.phenomenon: A scientist wants to determine the enthalpy change for the reaction C(s) + 2H2(g) -> CH4(g), but this reaction does not occur easily in a calorimeter. However, the enthalpies of combustion for carbon, hydrogen, and methane are well known and can be measured accurately.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the scientist can determine delta H for the target reaction by___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the combustion reactions and their known delta H values to demonstrate how they can be rearranged and combined to yield the target reaction.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to Hess's Law, ___ because enthalpy is a state function. The scientist can ___ the combustion reaction for methane and ___ it with the combustion reactions for carbon and hydrogen because___. The sum of the delta H values equals ___ because___.

lessons.title: Energy in Reactions Review and Performance Task
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can connect exothermic/endothermic classification, PE diagrams, calorimetry calculations, bond energy analysis, and Hess's Law to solve multi-step energy problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could invent a product that uses a chemical reaction to heat or cool something, what would it be and who would it help?
lessons.do_now: Without looking at your notes, sketch a PE diagram for an exothermic reaction with a catalyst. Label all five key features (reactants, products, Ea, Ea with catalyst, delta H).
materials: Reference tables: bond energies, specific heat capacities
Whiteboards and markers for group work

engage.description: Rapid-fire review: Teacher projects 10 quick statements and students hold up cards marked 'EXO' or 'ENDO' for each: ice melting, burning wood, cooking pasta, photosynthesis, rusting iron, baking soda and vinegar, cellular respiration, condensation of steam, decomposition of water by electrolysis, neutralization of acid and base.

explore.description: Performance task: Students receive a scenario about designing a camping meal heater. They must select between two chemical reactions (given thermochemical equations and bond energy data), calculate which releases more heat per gram using q = mCdeltaT and Hess's Law, draw PE diagrams for each, and write a recommendation with evidence.

explain.description: Gallery walk: Groups post their PE diagrams and calculations on whiteboards around the room. Students circulate, compare approaches, and note which calculation method (calorimetry vs. bond energy) each group used. Class discussion: Do both methods give the same answer? Why might they differ slightly?

elaborate.description: Cumulative practice: Students work through three multi-step problems that combine concepts: (1) Given a PE diagram, identify delta H and calculate heat released when 50 g of water absorbs that energy. (2) Use bond energies to verify a delta H value. (3) Apply Hess's Law with three equations.

evaluate.description: Unit 6 formative assessment: Five questions spanning all lesson topics — classification, PE diagram interpretation, calorimetry calculation, bond energy analysis, and Hess's Law application.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a unit concept map showing connections between exo/endo, PE diagrams, q=mCdeltaT, bond energies, and Hess's Law; include formula reference sheet for all calculations.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the performance task and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Extend the performance task by evaluating the environmental impact of each reaction option (byproducts, sustainability) and proposing a green chemistry alternative.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual concept summary sheet; allow oral explanation of performance task reasoning with written calculations; visual formula cards.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to three questions; provide formula sheet and worked example references; allow extended time; partner support during performance task.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the environmental justice implications of energy-producing chemical reactions in industrial settings. Highlight how communities near petroleum refineries and chemical plants (often communities of color, such as Cancer Alley in Louisiana) bear disproportionate health impacts from exothermic industrial processes. Connect to green chemistry initiatives led by scientists like John Warner, who co-founded the field of green chemistry to design reactions that minimize waste and hazardous byproducts.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Reactions transfer energy.' Students expand: 'Chemical reactions, which involve the breaking and forming of bonds between atoms, transfer energy between the system and surroundings in measurable quantities that can be calculated using calorimetry or predicted using bond energy data and Hess's Law.'

vocabulary.definition: The branch of chemistry that studies the heat energy changes associated with chemical reactions and physical changes
The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed from one form to another
The enthalpy change (delta H) that occurs during a chemical reaction at constant pressure
The design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances

Section 2: Review — Exo/Endo, PE Diagrams, Calorimetry
Section 3: Review — Bond Energy and Hess's Law
Section 4: Solving Multi-Step Energy Problems

cer.phenomenon: A company wants to develop a self-heating soup can. When the consumer pushes a button on the bottom of the can, two chemicals mix and heat the soup. The company is choosing between calcium oxide + water (delta H = -65 kJ/mol) and magnesium sulfate dissolution (delta H = -91 kJ/mol). Both reactions are exothermic, but the company must also consider safety, cost, and the amount of heat needed to raise 300 g of soup from 20 degrees C to 65 degrees C.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the company should choose ___ for the self-heating can because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the heat required to warm the soup using q = mCdeltaT, determine how many moles of each reactant would be needed, and compare the practicality of each option.
cer.reasoning_frame: The soup requires ___ joules of heat, calculated by___. Using reaction ___, the company would need ___ moles because___. This option is preferable because___, considering safety and cost factors such as___.

units.title: Reaction Rates & Equilibrium
units.anchoring_phenomenon: When you open a bottle of soda, it fizzes vigorously and goes flat over time. But if you recap the bottle tightly, the fizzing slows and eventually seems to stop — even though CO2 is still dissolved in the liquid. Why does the fizzing stop in a sealed bottle?
essential_questions: What conditions must be met for a chemical reaction to occur, and how can we control how fast it happens?
What does it mean for a chemical system to be in equilibrium, and how do changes in conditions shift the equilibrium?
How can we use equilibrium expressions to predict the relative amounts of reactants and products?
units.crse_theme: Students explore how reaction rates and equilibrium are embedded in cultural food practices — fermentation in West African, Korean, and Latin American cuisines, tea brewing across Asian cultures, and yogurt-making in Middle Eastern and South Asian traditions. Students also examine how Le Chatelier's principle applies to industrial chemistry and environmental justice issues like acid rain formation.

formative: Exit tickets on collision theory and rate factors

investigations: Investigation 7: Factors Affecting Reaction Rate — The Alka-Seltzer Experiment

lessons.title: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how collision theory accounts for reaction rates and predict how changing temperature, concentration, surface area, or adding a catalyst will affect the rate of a reaction.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a crowd of people trying to get through a doorway. What conditions make it faster or slower for everyone to get through?
lessons.do_now: A student drops a whole Alka-Seltzer tablet into cold water and a crushed tablet into hot water. Which setup will react faster? List as many reasons as you can.
materials: Alka-Seltzer tablets (whole and crushed, 8 per group)
Ice, room temperature water, and hot water
Hydrochloric acid at two concentrations: 0.5 M and 2.0 M (for teacher demo)

engage.description: Show a time-lapse video of iron rusting (very slow reaction) next to a video of an explosion (very fast reaction). Ask: Both are chemical reactions. What makes one take years and the other a fraction of a second? Students brainstorm factors that might affect how fast a reaction occurs and share with the class.

explore.description: Controlled experiment: Groups test how four factors affect the rate of Alka-Seltzer dissolving in water. Each group tests one variable while controlling others: (1) Temperature — cold vs. hot water with whole tablets; (2) Surface area — whole vs. crushed tablet in room-temp water; (3) Concentration — the teacher demos HCl at 0.5 M vs. 2.0 M reacting with zinc metal; (4) Catalyst — not tested directly but discussed. Groups record time to complete dissolution and calculate relative rates.

explain.description: Teacher introduces collision theory: for a reaction to occur, particles must (1) collide, (2) with sufficient energy (greater than or equal to activation energy), and (3) with proper orientation. Connect each factor to the theory: Higher temperature means faster particles and more energetic collisions. Higher concentration means more particles in the same space, so more frequent collisions. Greater surface area exposes more particles to collide. Catalysts lower Ea so more collisions have sufficient energy.

elaborate.description: Students analyze two Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves — one at low temperature and one at high temperature. They shade the area representing particles with energy greater than Ea and explain why increasing temperature dramatically increases reaction rate. They then sketch what happens when a catalyst lowers Ea on the same curve.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A factory produces ammonia gas. The plant manager wants to speed up the reaction. For each proposed change (raising temperature, increasing pressure/concentration of reactants, adding a catalyst), explain using collision theory WHY each would increase the rate.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a collision theory reference card with diagrams showing effective vs. ineffective collisions; pre-formatted data table for the Alka-Seltzer experiment with column headers filled in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the experimental investigation and collision theory analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design an additional experiment to quantify the relationship between temperature and rate — predict whether doubling temperature doubles the rate, and justify using collision theory and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
differentiation.ell: Visual collision theory diagrams with bilingual labels; sentence frames for explaining each factor: 'Increasing ___ causes the reaction rate to ___ because___.'
differentiation.iep: Assign one variable per group rather than rotating; provide a completed example of one factor's analysis; allow verbal explanation as alternative to written exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss traditional fermentation practices across cultures as examples of controlling reaction rate: Korean kimchi fermentation (temperature and salt concentration control the rate of bacterial activity), Ethiopian injera preparation (time and temperature for wild yeast fermentation), and Mexican pulque production. Highlight how these communities empirically controlled reaction rates for thousands of years before collision theory was formalized.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'reaction rate': Crushing a solid reactant increases the reaction rate because___. Both reactions use the same chemicals, but the one at higher temperature reacts faster, so___. A catalyst does not change the products of a reaction, but it does increase the rate because___.

vocabulary.definition: The speed at which reactants are converted to products, measured as the change in concentration over time
The theory that reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation
The minimum energy required for a collision to result in a reaction
A collision between reactant particles that has enough energy and the correct orientation to form products
The exposed outer area of a substance; increasing surface area increases the number of particles available for collisions
A substance that increases reaction rate by lowering activation energy without being consumed in the reaction

Section 2: Collision Theory — Three Requirements for a Reaction
Section 3: Factor 1 — Temperature and Kinetic Energy
Section 4: Factor 2 — Concentration and Collision Frequency
Section 5: Factor 3 — Surface Area and Exposure
Section 6: Factor 4 — Catalysts and Activation Energy

cer.phenomenon: A science supply company sells Alka-Seltzer tablets for classroom experiments. A teacher notices that when students use warm water, the tablets dissolve in about 20 seconds. With cold water, the same tablets take over 2 minutes. The teacher asks students to explain this observation using collision theory.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Alka-Seltzer dissolves faster in warm water because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use data from the class experiment (time to dissolve at different temperatures) and principles of collision theory to support your explanation.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to collision theory, a reaction occurs when particles collide with___. At higher temperatures, the water molecules have ___ kinetic energy, which means___. This results in ___ effective collisions per unit time, so the rate___.

lessons.title: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can interpret graphs showing changes in concentration or volume over time to determine reaction rate and identify when a reaction is complete.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time something started quickly and then slowed down — a phone battery draining, a song getting popular, traffic clearing. Why does the rate change over time?
lessons.do_now: A graph shows the volume of gas produced in a reaction over 5 minutes. The curve rises steeply at first, then levels off. What is happening to the reaction rate over time? Why might it slow down?
materials: Rate graph analysis worksheet with 4 different reaction graphs (printed)
Graph paper (for students to construct their own graphs)
Data set from Alka-Seltzer experiment (previous lesson)

engage.description: Project two graphs side by side: Graph A shows concentration of reactant decreasing over time; Graph B shows concentration of product increasing over time for the same reaction. Ask: What is the relationship between these two graphs? When one goes down, the other goes up — can students explain why using conservation of matter?

explore.description: Students analyze four different reaction rate graphs on their worksheet. For each graph, they: (1) identify whether the graph shows reactant consumption or product formation, (2) determine the time interval with the fastest rate (steepest slope), (3) estimate the rate during that interval (change in concentration divided by change in time), (4) identify when the reaction is essentially complete (curve flattens). They compare graphs showing the same reaction at two different temperatures.

explain.description: Teacher explains: The rate of a reaction at any moment equals the slope of the concentration vs. time curve. A steep slope means a fast rate; a flat slope means the reaction has slowed or stopped. Rate typically decreases over time because reactant concentration decreases, leading to fewer collisions. Students annotate their graphs with slope lines and rate labels.

elaborate.description: Students use their Alka-Seltzer data from the previous lesson to construct their own rate graph. They plot volume of gas produced vs. time, draw a best-fit curve, and calculate the average rate during the first 30 seconds and the last 30 seconds. They explain the difference using collision theory.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a graph showing gas volume produced over time for two trials — one with a catalyst and one without — students (1) identify which curve represents the catalyzed reaction and explain how they know, (2) compare the final gas volume for both trials, and (3) explain why a catalyst changes the rate but not the total amount of product.

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-labeled axes on graph paper with scale markings; include a step-by-step guide for calculating slope: 'Pick two points. Subtract the y-values. Subtract the x-values. Divide.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the graph analysis and graph construction as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate instantaneous rate by drawing tangent lines at three different points on their curve and compare to average rate over the same intervals.
differentiation.ell: Provide annotated example graph with bilingual labels for all axes and features; use sentence frames for graph description: 'Between ___ and ___ seconds, the rate is ___ because the slope is___.'
differentiation.iep: Reduce graphs to analyze from four to two; provide graph construction template with axes pre-drawn and data points partially plotted; allow partner work.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight the contributions of Jacobus van't Hoff, the first Nobel Prize winner in Chemistry (1901), who studied how temperature affects reaction rates. Connect to modern applications: pharmaceutical companies use rate data to determine drug shelf life and expiration dates — a topic of environmental justice since communities in low-income areas often have less access to fresh medications.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'The reaction rate, the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, can be determined by calculating the slope of a concentration-time graph.' 'The curve flattens at the end, an indication that the reaction has reached completion, because all of the limiting reactant has been consumed.'

vocabulary.definition: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, often expressed in mol/L per second
The steepness of a line on a graph, calculated as the change in y divided by the change in x; represents rate on a concentration-time graph
The overall change in concentration divided by the total time elapsed for a given interval
The rate of a reaction at a specific moment in time, determined by the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point

Section 2: Calculating Rate from Graph Data — The Slope Method
Section 3: Why Reaction Rate Decreases Over Time

cer.phenomenon: Two students study the same decomposition reaction. Student A runs the reaction at 25 degrees C and Student B runs it at 50 degrees C. Both plot concentration of reactant vs. time. Student A's curve decreases slowly and levels off at 300 seconds. Student B's curve decreases steeply and levels off at 90 seconds. Both curves level off at the same final concentration.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that temperature affects the rate but not the final amount of product because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the slopes and endpoints of both graphs and connect to collision theory to explain the observations.
cer.reasoning_frame: Student B's curve is steeper, meaning ___, because at higher temperature, particles have ___ kinetic energy and collisions are___. Both curves reach the same final concentration because ___, which shows that temperature affects ___ but not___.

lessons.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe dynamic equilibrium as the state where the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and explain why concentrations remain constant even though both reactions continue.
lessons.circle_prompt: Imagine a room where the same number of people enter through one door as leave through another every minute. The room always has about the same number of people. Is the room 'doing nothing' or is something happening?
lessons.do_now: A sealed bottle of soda appears to have stopped fizzing. But when you open it, CO2 escapes rapidly. Was the CO2 really 'gone' while the bottle was sealed, or was something else going on?
materials: Two graduated cylinders and two different-sized straws per group (equilibrium simulation)

engage.description: Sealed soda demo: Hold up a sealed bottle of clear soda. Ask: Is anything happening inside this bottle right now? Students may say no. Then shake it and open it — the vigorous fizzing proves CO2 was actively dissolving and un-dissolving even though it appeared static. Introduce the concept: at equilibrium, both forward and reverse processes occur continuously at equal rates.

explore.description: Straw transfer activity: Each group has two graduated cylinders — one filled with 50 mL of colored water (reactants) and one empty (products). Two students simultaneously transfer water between cylinders using different-sized straws (one large, one small). They record the volume in each cylinder every 30 seconds for 5 minutes. Initially, more water moves from the full to the empty cylinder, but as volumes equalize, the rates of transfer become closer until volumes stabilize.

explain.description: Teacher connects the activity to chemical equilibrium: the large straw represents the forward reaction and the small straw the reverse reaction. At first, the forward rate is greater because there are more 'reactant' particles. As products accumulate, the reverse rate increases. Equilibrium is reached when forward rate equals reverse rate. Key point: concentrations are constant but not necessarily equal — the system is dynamic, not static. Students draw equilibrium concentration-time graphs showing both reactants and products leveling off.

elaborate.description: Students examine the PhET equilibrium simulation, adjusting initial concentrations and observing how equilibrium position changes. They answer: If you start with more reactants, do you get more products at equilibrium? Does the system still reach a state where rates are equal? Students record observations and compare with their straw activity results.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A student says 'At equilibrium, the reaction has stopped because the concentrations aren't changing.' (1) Explain why this statement is incorrect. (2) Draw a rate-time graph showing the forward and reverse rates approaching equilibrium. (3) Label the point where equilibrium is established.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-drawn rate-time graph template with the forward rate curve started; include a checklist of equilibrium characteristics: 'At equilibrium: forward rate ___ reverse rate; concentrations are ___; reactions are still ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the straw transfer activity and graphing as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Predict how using two straws of the same size would change the equilibrium position and graph the expected concentration-time curves. Test the prediction with the simulation.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual dynamic/static equilibrium comparison chart with diagrams; use the straw analogy as a visual anchor throughout the lesson; sentence frames for exit ticket.
differentiation.iep: Partner with peer for straw activity; provide pre-formatted data table; allow verbal explanation for exit ticket question 1; reduce to two questions.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect equilibrium to the carbon cycle and ocean acidification — a critical environmental justice issue. As atmospheric CO2 increases, the equilibrium CO2(g) + H2O(l) -> H2CO3(aq) shifts right, making oceans more acidic. This disproportionately affects coastal fishing communities in the Global South, many of them indigenous or low-income. Highlight the work of Sylvia Earle, marine biologist and National Geographic Explorer, who has advocated for understanding ocean chemistry.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'dynamic equilibrium': At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant because___. The forward and reverse reactions are both still occurring, but the concentrations appear unchanged, so___. A sealed soda bottle appears to have stopped fizzing, but CO2 molecules are still dissolving and escaping because___.

vocabulary.definition: A chemical reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions
The state in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
The reaction that proceeds from reactants to products as written in the chemical equation
The reaction that proceeds from products back to reactants
A system that can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings; required for equilibrium to be established

Section 2: What is Dynamic Equilibrium?
Section 3: Rate-Time Graphs — Watching Equilibrium Develop
Section 4: Concentration-Time Graphs at Equilibrium
Section 5: Equilibrium is Dynamic, Not Static

cer.phenomenon: A sealed container holds nitrogen dioxide (NO2, a brown gas) in equilibrium with dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4, a colorless gas) according to the equation 2NO2(g) <-> N2O4(g). A student observes that the brown color in the sealed tube does not change over several hours. The student concludes that all the NO2 has reacted and the reaction is complete.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's conclusion is incorrect because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the definition of dynamic equilibrium and evidence from the straw transfer activity to explain why the color remains constant while both reactions continue.
cer.reasoning_frame: The constant brown color indicates that the concentration of NO2 is___. However, this does not mean the reaction has stopped because at equilibrium, the forward reaction (NO2 -> N2O4) occurs at the same rate as___. If we could track individual molecules, we would see___.

lessons.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can predict how changes in concentration, temperature, or pressure will shift a system at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a time when something in your life was balanced and then something changed — a new sibling, moving to a new school, a schedule change. How did things adjust to find a new normal?
lessons.do_now: The equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) <-> 2NH3(g) + heat exists in a sealed container. If we suddenly add more N2, predict what will happen to the amount of NH3. Explain your reasoning.
materials: NO2/N2O4 sealed tubes in hot and cold water baths (demo)
CoCl2 equilibrium color change demo materials (cobalt chloride, HCl, water)

engage.description: Demo: Place sealed tubes containing the NO2/N2O4 equilibrium mixture into hot water and ice water. Students observe the tube in hot water becoming darker brown (more NO2) and the tube in cold water becoming lighter (more N2O4). Ask: The same chemicals are in both tubes. Why does temperature change the color? Introduce Le Chatelier: when a stress is applied, the system shifts to counteract the stress.

explore.description: Prediction activity: Students work in groups with whiteboards. Teacher presents a series of equilibrium systems with specific stresses applied. For each, groups predict the direction of shift (left, right, or no change) and explain their reasoning: (1) Adding more reactant, (2) Removing product, (3) Increasing temperature for an exothermic reaction, (4) Decreasing volume (increasing pressure) for a reaction with more gas moles on one side. After each prediction, teacher reveals the answer and class discusses.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes Le Chatelier's principle: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a stress (change in concentration, temperature, or pressure), the system shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the stress. Key rules: (1) Adding a substance shifts away from it; removing shifts toward it. (2) Increasing temperature shifts toward the endothermic direction; decreasing shifts toward exothermic. (3) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer moles of gas. (4) A catalyst does NOT shift equilibrium — it only speeds up reaching equilibrium.

elaborate.description: Application: The Haber process for making ammonia (N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, exothermic). Students determine optimal conditions to maximize ammonia yield: high pressure (4 gas moles -> 2 gas moles), low temperature (favors exothermic direction), but low temperature slows the rate. Industrial compromise: moderate temperature with a catalyst. Students explain why each condition helps or hinders.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: For the reaction 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g) + heat, predict and explain the effect on equilibrium of: (1) adding more O2, (2) increasing temperature, (3) decreasing the volume of the container, (4) adding a catalyst.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Le Chatelier's decision flowchart: 'Was a substance added? -> Shift away from it. Was temperature increased? -> Is the reaction exo or endo? -> Shift toward endo.' Include color-coded arrows on the prediction worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the prediction activity and Haber process analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on one industrial application of Le Chatelier's principle (Contact process for sulfuric acid, or Ostwald process for nitric acid) and explain the economic trade-offs between yield and rate.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual Le Chatelier's principle reference card with arrow diagrams in English and native language; use the analogy of a seesaw to represent equilibrium shifts.
differentiation.iep: Reduce exit ticket stresses from four to two; provide Le Chatelier's rule card for reference; allow partner work during prediction activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Haber-Bosch process in its historical context: Fritz Haber developed the process to fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for fertilizer, feeding billions but also enabling explosives in World War I. Highlight the ethical complexity of scientific discoveries. Also connect to acid rain: the equilibrium SO2 + H2O <-> H2SO3 shifts right with increased SO2 pollution, disproportionately affecting communities near coal-burning power plants — many of which are located in low-income areas and communities of color.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Le Chatelier's principle': Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right because___. Increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction, but industries want maximum product yield, so they must find a compromise because___. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium, so___.

vocabulary.definition: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a stress, the system shifts in the direction that partially relieves the stress
A change in concentration, temperature, or pressure that disturbs a system at equilibrium
The equilibrium moves toward producing more products (forward reaction is favored)
The equilibrium moves toward producing more reactants (reverse reaction is favored)
The industrial process for synthesizing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gases under high pressure with a catalyst

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Le Chatelier's Principle — Responding to Stress
Section 2: Effect of Changing Concentration
Section 3: Effect of Changing Temperature
Section 4: Effect of Changing Pressure/Volume
Section 5: The Haber Process — Le Chatelier in Industry

cer.phenomenon: A chemical plant produces sulfur trioxide (SO3) using the Contact process: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g), delta H = -198 kJ. The plant operates at 450 degrees C with a vanadium pentoxide catalyst. A new engineer proposes lowering the temperature to 200 degrees C to increase the yield of SO3, since the reaction is exothermic.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the engineer's proposal would increase the equilibrium yield of SO3 but is NOT practical because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain the equilibrium shift, and collision theory to explain why lowering temperature creates a rate problem.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to Le Chatelier's principle, decreasing temperature for an exothermic reaction shifts equilibrium toward ___ because___. However, at 200 degrees C, the reaction rate would ___ because___. The current temperature of 450 degrees C is a compromise between ___ and___.

lessons.title: Equilibrium Expressions and Keq
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write an equilibrium expression (Keq) for a reversible reaction and use the value of Keq to predict whether products or reactants are favored at equilibrium.
lessons.circle_prompt: If a scoreboard shows one team leading 75-25, what do you know about the game? What if the score is 50-48? What does the ratio tell you?
lessons.do_now: Two reversible reactions are at equilibrium. Reaction A has mostly products and very little reactants. Reaction B has mostly reactants and very little products. Which reaction has gone 'further' toward completion? How could we use a number to describe this?
materials: Concentration data tables for 5 equilibrium systems (printed)

engage.description: Ratio analogy: Show two photos — a stadium that is 90% full (products favored, Keq much greater than 1) and a nearly empty stadium with most people still outside (reactants favored, Keq much less than 1). Ask: If the ratio of people inside to people outside is large, what does that mean? Introduce Keq as the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium.

explore.description: Students receive concentration data for five equilibrium systems at a given temperature. For each, they calculate the ratio [products]/[reactants] in various ways until they discover that the correct equilibrium expression uses concentrations raised to the power of their coefficients. Teacher guides: For aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Keq = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b. Students verify this formula gives a consistent Keq value from different data sets for the same reaction.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: Keq is the equilibrium constant expression. Rules: (1) Products in numerator, reactants in denominator. (2) Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient. (3) Pure solids and liquids are NOT included (their concentrations are constant). (4) Keq greater than 1 means products are favored; Keq less than 1 means reactants are favored; Keq approximately equal to 1 means comparable amounts. (5) Keq changes only with temperature.

elaborate.description: Practice: Students write Keq expressions for five reactions, including ones with solids and liquids that must be excluded. Then they calculate Keq from given concentration data and interpret: Is this system product-favored or reactant-favored? They also examine solubility equilibrium (Ksp) as a special case where a solid dissolves.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the Keq expression for N2(g) + 3H2(g) <-> 2NH3(g). (2) At a certain temperature, [N2] = 0.50 M, [H2] = 0.30 M, and [NH3] = 0.20 M. Calculate Keq. (3) Is this system product-favored or reactant-favored? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Keq expression template: 'Numerator: [product 1]^coeff x [product 2]^coeff. Denominator: [reactant 1]^coeff x [reactant 2]^coeff.' Include a worked example side-by-side with each practice problem.
differentiation.on_level: Complete Keq expression writing, calculations, and interpretations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given Keq values at two different temperatures for the same reaction, determine whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain using Le Chatelier's principle.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual Keq expression builder with color-coded products (green) and reactants (red); bilingual interpretation guide for Keq values; sentence frames for explanations.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems from five to three; provide formula card with Keq template; allow calculator for all work; partner for expression writing.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the work of Cato Maximilian Guldberg and Peter Waage, Norwegian scientists who formulated the law of mass action in 1864, establishing the mathematical basis for equilibrium expressions. Connect to how solubility equilibrium (Ksp) relates to water hardness — a practical chemistry issue affecting communities worldwide. In many developing nations, understanding mineral solubility in water sources is essential for safe drinking water.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'equilibrium constant': The Keq value for this reaction is much greater than 1 because___. Both reactions are at equilibrium, but Reaction A has a Keq of 5000 while Reaction B has a Keq of 0.002, so___. Pure solids are not included in the Keq expression because___.

vocabulary.definition: A numerical value that expresses the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to the power of their coefficients
The mathematical formula Keq = [products]^coefficients / [reactants]^coefficients for a given reaction
A reaction where Keq is greater than 1, meaning products are present in higher concentrations than reactants at equilibrium
A reaction where Keq is less than 1, meaning reactants are present in higher concentrations than products at equilibrium
The equilibrium constant for the dissolving of a slightly soluble ionic compound in water

Section 2: Writing Keq Expressions from Balanced Equations
Section 3: Rules — Excluding Solids and Liquids
Section 4: Calculating Keq from Concentration Data
Section 5: Interpreting Keq — Products vs. Reactants Favored

cer.phenomenon: At 25 degrees C, the reaction N2O4(g) <-> 2NO2(g) has a Keq of 4.6 x 10^-3. At 100 degrees C, the Keq for the same reaction is 0.36. The forward reaction is endothermic.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that increasing temperature increases the value of Keq for this reaction because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the Keq values at both temperatures and Le Chatelier's principle to explain the relationship between temperature and Keq for an endothermic reaction.
cer.reasoning_frame: At 25 degrees C, Keq is very small, meaning ___ are favored. At 100 degrees C, Keq is larger, meaning more ___ are present. This is consistent with Le Chatelier's principle because increasing temperature for an endothermic reaction shifts equilibrium toward ___, which increases the ___ in the numerator of the Keq expression.

lessons.title: Rates and Equilibrium Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply collision theory, Le Chatelier's principle, and equilibrium expressions to analyze complex reaction systems and solve multi-step problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: Share a food or drink that changes when you add something to it — like lemon in tea or salt on a watermelon. What happens and why do you think it changes?
lessons.do_now: For the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) <-> CH3OH(g) + heat: (1) Write the Keq expression. (2) Predict what happens to Keq if temperature increases. (3) Predict the effect on the amount of CH3OH if more H2 is added.
materials: Equilibrium scenario cards (set of 12 for group activity)

engage.description: Rapid review game: Teacher reads equilibrium scenarios and students respond with hand signals: thumbs up for shift right, thumbs down for shift left, flat hand for no change. Scenarios include changes in concentration, temperature, pressure, and addition of catalysts. Keep pace fast to build fluency.

explore.description: Scenario card activity: Groups receive complex equilibrium scenario cards that require integrating multiple concepts. Example: 'A factory runs the reaction A(g) + B(g) <-> 2C(g), delta H = +150 kJ. Current Keq = 0.05. The manager wants more product C. Evaluate three proposals: (1) increase temperature, (2) increase pressure, (3) add a catalyst. For each, predict the effect on rate, equilibrium position, and Keq value.' Groups present their analyses on whiteboards.

explain.description: Class discussion synthesizing key distinctions: (1) Rate vs. equilibrium — catalysts affect rate but not equilibrium position. (2) Le Chatelier shifts are temporary adjustments — the system reaches a new equilibrium. (3) Only temperature changes Keq. Students complete a concept map linking collision theory, rate factors, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, and Keq.

elaborate.description: Multi-step problems: Students solve three problems that combine rate and equilibrium concepts. Example: Given a rate graph and equilibrium data, students identify the point where equilibrium is reached, calculate Keq, then predict how a specified stress would change the graph.

evaluate.description: Unit 7 formative assessment: Six questions covering collision theory, rate factors, rate graphs, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, and Keq calculations.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a completed concept map as a reference tool during the review; include a summary card with all major rules (collision theory, Le Chatelier, Keq rules).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the scenario analysis and multi-step problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a real industrial equilibrium system (ammonia synthesis or sulfuric acid production) using actual operating conditions and Keq data, and write a recommendation for optimizing yield.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual concept map with visual icons; allow oral presentation of scenario card analysis; provide sentence frames for written responses.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide reference cards for all major concepts; allow extended time; partner support during scenario activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how traditional fermentation processes in West African, Korean, and Latin American cuisines represent empirical understanding of reaction rates and equilibrium. Highlight how Korean onggi pottery is specifically designed with porous walls that allow air exchange, controlling the rate and equilibrium of kimchi fermentation. Connect to the work of Lloyd Hall, an African American chemist who revolutionized food preservation by understanding how to control reaction rates to prevent spoilage.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Equilibrium shifts.' Students expand: 'When a system at dynamic equilibrium experiences a stress such as a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the stress, eventually establishing a new equilibrium with different concentrations but at the same Keq value if temperature is unchanged.'

vocabulary.definition: The specific set of concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium for a given set of conditions
The principle that at equilibrium, the ratio of product to reactant concentrations (each raised to their coefficients) is constant at a given temperature
A change in the relative amounts of reactants and products in response to a stress, as predicted by Le Chatelier's principle
The balancing of reaction rate and equilibrium yield in manufacturing, often choosing moderate conditions with catalysts

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Connecting Rate and Equilibrium Concepts
Section 2: Review — Collision Theory and Rate Factors
Section 3: Review — Le Chatelier's Principle Applications
Section 4: Review — Writing and Calculating Keq

cer.phenomenon: A chemical company manufactures methanol (CH3OH) using the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) <-> CH3OH(g), delta H = -90 kJ. Current operating conditions are 250 degrees C and 100 atm with a copper-zinc catalyst. A consultant recommends switching to 100 degrees C to increase yield.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the consultant's recommendation would ___ the equilibrium yield of methanol but would ___ the production rate because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use Le Chatelier's principle to predict the equilibrium shift and collision theory to predict the effect on rate. Explain why the current conditions represent an industrial compromise.
cer.reasoning_frame: Lowering the temperature would shift equilibrium ___ because___, increasing the equilibrium concentration of methanol. However, at 100 degrees C, the rate of the reaction would ___ because___. The current conditions of 250 degrees C with a catalyst represent a compromise between ___ and___.

units.title: Acids, Bases & Salts
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Antacid tablets relieve heartburn by reacting with stomach acid. But if you take too many, your stomach can become too basic and you feel just as bad. How do chemists measure and control the balance between acids and bases?
essential_questions: What makes a substance an acid or a base, and how do different theories define them?
How does the pH scale quantify the strength of an acid or base, and what do pH values tell us about hydronium ion concentration?
What happens at the molecular level during a neutralization reaction, and what products are formed?
units.crse_theme: Students explore acids and bases through cultural and environmental lenses — the chemistry of traditional food preservation (pickling in vinegar across many cultures, lime in nixtamalization), the pH of natural dyes used in textile traditions from India and Central America, and the environmental justice implications of acid rain on communities near industrial zones.
investigations: Investigation 8: Acid-Base Titration — Determining the Concentration of an Unknown Acid

lessons.title: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define acids and bases according to both the Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry theories and identify conjugate acid-base pairs in a reaction.
lessons.circle_prompt: What sour foods do you enjoy? What about bitter foods? Do you know what makes them taste that way?
lessons.do_now: Look at these three formulas: HCl, NaOH, NaCl. One is an acid, one is a base, and one is a salt. Sort them and explain what pattern in the formulas helped you decide.
materials: pH test strips and solutions set: lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, ammonia, milk, soapy water (1 set per group)
Litmus paper (red and blue, 1 pack per group)
Safety goggles and gloves (1 per student)

engage.description: Mystery solution challenge: Show six clear, colorless solutions in labeled beakers (A through F). Tell students three are acids and three are bases, but they all look the same. Ask: Without tasting (never taste chemicals!), how could you tell them apart? Students brainstorm methods. Introduce the idea that acids and bases have different properties that can be tested.

explore.description: Station testing: Groups rotate through six solutions (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, ammonia solution, milk, soapy water). At each station, they test with red litmus paper, blue litmus paper, and pH strips. They record results in a data table and classify each as acid, base, or neutral. Students look for patterns: What do all acids have in common? All bases?

explain.description: Teacher introduces two definitions. Arrhenius: An acid produces H+ ions (hydronium, H3O+) in water; a base produces OH- ions in water. Bronsted-Lowry (broader): An acid is a proton (H+) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Students identify conjugate acid-base pairs in reactions like HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl- (HCl donates H+ to H2O, so HCl is the acid and H2O is the base; H3O+ and Cl- are the conjugate acid and conjugate base).

elaborate.description: Students classify 8 reactions using both Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions and identify conjugate pairs. They encounter an example where Bronsted-Lowry works but Arrhenius does not (e.g., NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl, no water involved) to understand why the Bronsted-Lowry definition is more broadly applicable.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Define acid and base according to the Bronsted-Lowry theory. (2) In the reaction NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base. (3) Explain why NH3 is a base even though it does not contain OH-.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Venn diagram comparing Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions; include a color-coded conjugate pair identification guide with arrows showing proton transfer.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the solution testing and conjugate pair analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research amphoteric substances (like water and amino acids) and explain how the same substance can act as both an acid and a base depending on the reaction partner.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual acid-base vocabulary cards with molecular diagrams; use color-coded arrows (red for proton donated, blue for proton accepted) in all examples; sentence frames for classification.
