differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted data table with litmus results partially filled in; reduce conjugate pair practice to 4 reactions; provide labeled example to reference.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the traditional use of natural acid-base indicators across cultures: red cabbage juice indicators used in European folk chemistry, turmeric as an indicator in Indian traditions (turns red in basic solutions), and the use of wood ash (basic) in West African indigo dyeing to set the dye. Highlight Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist whose acid-base theory was initially rejected as his doctoral thesis — he later won the Nobel Prize for it.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Bronsted-Lowry acid': HCl is a Bronsted-Lowry acid because___. Water can act as either an acid or a base, but in this reaction it accepts a proton, so___. The Arrhenius definition only applies to reactions in water, but the Bronsted-Lowry definition is broader because___.

vocabulary.definition: A substance that produces hydrogen ions (H+) or hydronium ions (H3O+) when dissolved in water
A substance that produces hydroxide ions (OH-) when dissolved in water
A proton (H+) donor in a chemical reaction
A proton (H+) acceptor in a chemical reaction
Two species that differ by one proton (H+); when an acid donates H+, it becomes its conjugate base, and when a base accepts H+, it becomes its conjugate acid
The ion formed when a hydrogen ion (H+) combines with a water molecule; present in all acidic solutions

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Properties of Acids and Bases
Section 2: Arrhenius Theory — Acids Produce H+, Bases Produce OH-
Section 3: Bronsted-Lowry Theory — Proton Donors and Acceptors
Section 4: Identifying Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
Section 5: Comparing the Two Theories

cer.phenomenon: A student tests household ammonia (NH3 dissolved in water) and finds that it turns red litmus blue, has a pH of 11, and feels slippery. However, ammonia's formula does not contain OH-. A classmate claims that ammonia cannot be a base because it has no hydroxide ions.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that ammonia IS a base even though its formula does not contain OH- because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the litmus and pH data, the equation NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, and the Bronsted-Lowry definition to explain.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to the Arrhenius definition, a base must ___. While NH3 does not contain OH- directly, when it dissolves in water it ___ because___. Under the Bronsted-Lowry definition, NH3 is a base because it ___ from water, making NH3 a proton ___ and water a proton___.

lessons.title: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can use the pH scale to classify solutions as acidic, basic, or neutral and calculate pH from hydronium ion concentration.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to rank your five favorite drinks from most sour to least sour, what order would they be in? What do you think is chemically different about the sour ones?
lessons.do_now: Solution A has a pH of 2 and Solution B has a pH of 5. A student says Solution A is 3 times more acidic than Solution B. Is this correct? Explain your reasoning.
materials: pH paper and pH meters or probes (1 per group)
Solution set: 0.1 M HCl, 0.01 M HCl, 0.001 M HCl, distilled water, 0.001 M NaOH, 0.01 M NaOH, 0.1 M NaOH
Indicator solution set: phenolphthalein, bromthymol blue, methyl orange, litmus

engage.description: Show a large pH scale poster with common substances plotted (battery acid at 1, lemon juice at 2, vinegar at 3, coffee at 5, milk at 6.5, pure water at 7, baking soda at 9, ammonia at 11, bleach at 13). Ask students to identify the pattern. Reveal: each step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in H3O+ concentration — pH is logarithmic. So Solution A (pH 2) is actually 1000 times more acidic than Solution B (pH 5).

explore.description: Two-part exploration. Part A: Students measure the pH of seven solutions (serial dilutions of HCl, water, and serial dilutions of NaOH) using pH paper and record results. They notice the pH changes by 1 for each tenfold dilution. Part B: Students test the same solutions with four indicators (phenolphthalein, bromthymol blue, methyl orange, litmus) and record the color at each pH. They construct an indicator reference chart showing the color-change range of each indicator.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: pH = -log[H3O+]. At pH 7, [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-7 M (neutral). Below 7 is acidic (more H3O+). Above 7 is basic (less H3O+, more OH-). Also: [H3O+] x [OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C (Kw). Students practice converting between pH and [H3O+]: If [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-3, pH = 3. If pH = 9, [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-9.

elaborate.description: Application problems: (1) A lake has a pH of 4.5 due to acid rain. Calculate [H3O+]. (2) A student measures [OH-] = 1 x 10^-4 M. Find [H3O+] and pH. (3) Which indicator from the reference chart would be best for detecting whether milk (pH ~6.5) has become acidic (spoiled)? Justify your choice using the indicator ranges.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the pH of a solution with [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-5 M. (2) A solution has a pH of 11. Calculate [H3O+] and [OH-]. (3) How many times more acidic is a solution with pH 3 than a solution with pH 6?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pH conversion chart showing pH values from 1-14 with corresponding [H3O+] concentrations already listed; include step-by-step calculation template: 'pH = -log[___] = -log[1 x 10^-___] = ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the pH measurement, indicator charting, and calculation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate pH for concentrations that are not exact powers of 10 (e.g., [H3O+] = 3.5 x 10^-4 M) using the log function on a calculator, and explain why pH is not always a whole number.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual pH scale with color coding and bilingual labels; use sentence frames for explaining calculations; allow verbal explanation of indicator choices.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-formatted calculation workspace with blanks to fill in; allow use of pH conversion chart during exit ticket; reduce problems from three to two.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss acid rain as an environmental justice issue: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from coal plants and factories create acid rain that lowers the pH of lakes and soil. Communities in Appalachia and the Adirondacks have experienced ecological damage. Highlight how pH monitoring helped advocate for the Clean Air Act. Also discuss how soil pH affects agriculture — the traditional practice of adding lime (CaO, a base) to acidic soil has been used by farmers worldwide for centuries, from Roman agriculture to modern sustainable farming.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'pH': A solution with pH 2 is more acidic than a solution with pH 5 because___. Both solutions are acidic, but the one with pH 2 has 1000 times more hydronium ions, so___. The pH scale is logarithmic, so each one-unit change represents___.

vocabulary.definition: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures the concentration of hydronium ions in a solution; pH = -log[H3O+]
A solution with a pH below 7, containing more H3O+ ions than OH- ions
A solution with a pH above 7, containing more OH- ions than H3O+ ions
A solution with a pH of 7, where [H3O+] equals [OH-], each at 1 x 10^-7 M
A substance that changes color at a specific pH range, used to estimate the pH of a solution
The product of [H3O+] and [OH-] in water, always equal to 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The pH Scale — Logarithmic and Powerful
Section 2: Calculating pH from [H3O+]
Section 3: The Relationship Between [H3O+] and [OH-]
Section 4: Indicators — Choosing the Right One for the Job
Section 5: pH in the Real World — Acid Rain, Soil, and Body Chemistry

cer.phenomenon: A blueberry farmer tests soil pH and gets a reading of 8.0. Blueberries grow best in soil with pH between 4.5 and 5.0. The farmer adds elemental sulfur to the soil, which bacteria oxidize to produce sulfuric acid according to the reaction: 2S + 3O2 + 2H2O -> 2H2SO4.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that adding sulfur will ___ the soil pH to the optimal range because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the pH scale, the reaction equation, and knowledge of acids to explain how sulfur addition changes [H3O+] and therefore pH.
cer.reasoning_frame: The current pH of 8.0 means the soil is ___, with [H3O+] = ___. The farmer needs to ___ the pH, which requires ___ the [H3O+]. The sulfur is oxidized to ___, which is a strong acid that ___ in water to produce ___ ions, thereby ___ the pH.

lessons.title: Neutralization Reactions and Titration
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write balanced equations for neutralization reactions, predict the products (salt + water), and determine the concentration of an unknown acid or base using titration data.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever used baking soda to clean something or to settle an upset stomach? What do you think it does chemically?
lessons.do_now: If you mix equal amounts of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH), what do you think will happen to the pH? Will the mixture be acidic, basic, or neutral? Explain.
materials: Titration data table and calculation worksheet (printed)
Safety goggles, gloves, and aprons (1 per student)

engage.description: Demo: Teacher adds a few drops of phenolphthalein to NaOH solution (turns pink). Then slowly adds HCl drop by drop while students count. At the equivalence point, the pink color disappears. Ask: What happened? Where did the base go? How many drops of acid did it take to 'cancel out' the base? Introduce the concept of neutralization.

explore.description: Titration lab: Students perform a titration of an unknown concentration HCl with standardized 0.1 M NaOH. Using a burette, they add NaOH to the acid (with phenolphthalein) until a persistent pink color appears. They record the volume of NaOH used, repeat for two more trials, and calculate the average. Then they use the equation M1V1 = M2V2 (for 1:1 mole ratio) to determine the molarity of the unknown HCl.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes neutralization: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water. For Arrhenius: H+ + OH- -> H2O. The salt is formed from the cation of the base and the anion of the acid. Students write balanced equations for: HCl + NaOH, H2SO4 + KOH, HNO3 + Ca(OH)2. Teacher explains the titration calculation: at the equivalence point, moles of acid = moles of base (adjusted for stoichiometry).

elaborate.description: Students solve titration problems: (1) 25.0 mL of H2SO4 is neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH. Find the molarity of the acid (note: 2:1 mole ratio). (2) Identify the salt produced in each of the three neutralization reactions from the Explain phase. (3) Predict the pH at the equivalence point for a strong acid-strong base titration.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced equation for the neutralization of phosphoric acid (H3PO4) with sodium hydroxide (NaOH). (2) In a titration, 20.0 mL of 0.15 M HCl is neutralized by 15.0 mL of NaOH. Calculate the concentration of NaOH. (3) Name the salt produced.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a neutralization equation template: '___ acid + ___ base -> ___ salt + H2O.' Include a step-by-step titration calculation guide with a worked example showing MaVa = MbVb.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the titration lab and calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a titration curve (pH vs. volume of base added) to identify the equivalence point, half-equivalence point, and buffer region. Compare strong acid/strong base curves with weak acid/strong base curves.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual step-by-step titration procedure with photographs; bilingual calculation templates; color-coded equation balancing guide (acid in red, base in blue, salt in green, water in black).
differentiation.iep: Partner for burette readings; provide pre-balanced equations for practice; reduce titration calculations to one trial; allow extended time; enlarged data table.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how antacid medications use neutralization reactions — calcium carbonate (Tums), magnesium hydroxide (Milk of Magnesia), and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) all neutralize excess stomach acid (HCl). Connect to traditional remedies across cultures: the use of alkaline mineral waters for digestive relief in many European and Middle Eastern traditions. Highlight Alice Ball, an African American chemist at the University of Hawaii who developed the first effective treatment for leprosy using chaulmoogra oil — her work involved understanding acid-base chemistry of organic compounds. She died at 24, and her male colleague initially took credit for her work.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'neutralization': When an acid reacts with a base, a salt and water are formed because___. Both HCl and H2SO4 are acids, but H2SO4 requires twice as much NaOH to neutralize it because___. The phenolphthalein turned from pink to clear, so we know___.

vocabulary.definition: A chemical reaction in which an acid and a base react to produce a salt and water
An ionic compound formed from the cation of a base and the anion of an acid during neutralization
A laboratory procedure in which a solution of known concentration is used to determine the concentration of an unknown solution
The point in a titration where the moles of acid exactly equal the moles of base
A graduated glass tube with a stopcock used to deliver precise volumes of liquid during a titration
A solution of known, precise concentration used in titrations

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is Neutralization? — Acid + Base = Salt + Water
Section 2: Writing Balanced Neutralization Equations
Section 3: Naming the Salt Products
Section 4: Titration — The Laboratory Technique
Section 5: Calculating Concentration from Titration Data

cer.phenomenon: A swimming pool manager measures the pool water pH at 8.5, which is too basic and can cause eye irritation. The manager adds muriatic acid (HCl) to lower the pH. After adding acid, the pH drops to 7.4. A swimmer asks: 'If you added acid to the pool, won't the chloride ions from HCl be harmful?'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the chloride ions from the added HCl are not harmful at these concentrations because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the neutralization reaction between HCl and the basic compounds in pool water, knowledge of salt formation, and the small concentrations involved.
cer.reasoning_frame: When HCl is added to basic pool water, it reacts with ___ to form ___ and water. The chloride ions produced are the same ions found in ___, which is already added to pools. The small volume of acid needed to change the pH from 8.5 to 7.4 produces a very ___ concentration of Cl- because___.

lessons.title: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can predict whether a salt solution will be acidic, basic, or neutral based on the identities of the parent acid and base, and apply all acid-base concepts to solve multi-step problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time when mixing two things that seemed neutral created something unexpected — like mixing ingredients in cooking that changed the flavor in a surprising way.
lessons.do_now: Sodium chloride (NaCl) dissolved in water has a pH of 7. Sodium acetate (NaCH3COO) dissolved in water has a pH of about 9. Both are salts. Why might one salt solution be neutral and the other basic?
materials: Salt solution set: NaCl, NaCH3COO, NH4Cl, Na2CO3, KNO3 (0.1 M each)
pH paper or meters (1 per group)

engage.description: Testing salt solutions: Each group tests the pH of five salt solutions and records whether each is acidic, basic, or neutral. Results are surprising — some salts produce acidic solutions, some basic, and some neutral. Ask: What determines the pH of a salt solution if the salt itself is ionic and seems 'neutral'?

explore.description: Pattern analysis: Students organize the five salts by identifying the parent acid and parent base for each (e.g., NaCl comes from HCl + NaOH). They classify each parent as strong or weak. They discover the pattern: salt of strong acid + strong base = neutral; salt of weak acid + strong base = basic; salt of strong acid + weak base = acidic. Students test this pattern against their pH data.

explain.description: Teacher explains hydrolysis: when a salt dissolves, its ions can react with water. If the anion comes from a weak acid, it acts as a base (accepts H+ from water, producing OH-). If the cation comes from a weak base, it acts as an acid (donates H+ to water, producing H3O+). Students write hydrolysis equations for acetate ion and ammonium ion to see this in action.

elaborate.description: Cumulative review: Students complete multi-step problems that integrate all Unit 8 concepts. Example: Identify the acid, base, salt, and water in a neutralization reaction; write the equation; predict the pH of the salt solution; calculate the concentration of the acid from titration data.

evaluate.description: Unit 8 formative assessment: Six questions covering Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions, pH calculations, neutralization equations, titration calculations, and salt hydrolysis predictions.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a salt hydrolysis decision tree: 'What is the parent acid? Strong or weak? What is the parent base? Strong or weak? Use the chart to predict pH.' Include a reference table of common strong acids and bases.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the salt testing, pattern analysis, and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the pH of a salt solution quantitatively using Ka and Kb values, and explain buffer systems (how a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base resists pH change).
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual strong acid/base reference list; visual hydrolysis reaction diagrams with arrows showing proton transfer; sentence frames for predictions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide all reference charts during assessment; allow partner work for salt testing; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of traditional soap-making across cultures — wood ash (potassium carbonate, a basic salt from hydrolysis) combined with animal fats in a saponification reaction. This process has been practiced for millennia in African, European, and Middle Eastern cultures. Highlight the tradition of black soap (ose dudu) from West Africa, where cocoa pod ash provides the alkaline solution needed for saponification. Also discuss how blood pH is maintained at 7.35-7.45 through buffer systems, and how understanding acid-base chemistry is critical in medicine.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Salts affect pH.' Students expand: 'Salts formed from the neutralization of acids and bases affect the pH of their aqueous solutions through a process called hydrolysis, in which the ions of the salt react with water molecules to produce either hydronium or hydroxide ions, depending on whether the parent acid or parent base was weak.'

vocabulary.definition: The reaction of an ion from a dissolved salt with water, which can produce either H3O+ or OH- and affect the pH of the solution
An acid that ionizes completely in water, producing a high concentration of H3O+ ions (e.g., HCl, HNO3, H2SO4)
An acid that only partially ionizes in water, establishing an equilibrium between molecules and ions (e.g., CH3COOH, HF)
A base that dissociates completely in water, producing a high concentration of OH- ions (e.g., NaOH, KOH)
A base that only partially ionizes in water (e.g., NH3)
A substance that can act as either an acid or a base depending on the reaction (e.g., water, amino acids)

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Salt Formation — What Salt Comes from Which Acid and Base?
Section 2: Predicting the pH of Salt Solutions — The Parent Acid/Base Method
Section 3: Hydrolysis — How Salt Ions React with Water
Section 4: Cumulative Review — Acids, Bases, pH, Neutralization, and Salts

cer.phenomenon: A student dissolves equal masses of sodium chloride (NaCl) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) each in 100 mL of distilled water. The NaCl solution has a pH of 7.0, but the Na2CO3 solution has a pH of 11.5. The student is confused because both are salts and should be 'neutral.'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the Na2CO3 solution is basic because___.
cer.evidence_source: Identify the parent acid and parent base of each salt, classify them as strong or weak, and write the hydrolysis equation for the carbonate ion.
cer.reasoning_frame: NaCl is formed from ___ (strong acid) and ___ (strong base), so neither ion hydrolyzes and the solution is___. Na2CO3 is formed from ___ (weak acid) and ___ (strong base). The carbonate ion (CO3 2-) reacts with water: CO3 2- + H2O -> ___ + ___, producing ___ ions, which makes the solution___.

units.title: Redox & Electrochemistry
units.anchoring_phenomenon: The Statue of Liberty was originally the color of a shiny copper penny. Over decades, it turned green. Meanwhile, the iron framework inside rusted and weakened. Both changes involve the same type of reaction — a transfer of electrons. What determines which metals lose electrons and which gain them?
essential_questions: How do we identify oxidation and reduction in a chemical reaction, and why must they always occur together?
How can the activity series predict whether a redox reaction will occur spontaneously?
How do electrochemical cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy, and how does electrolysis do the reverse?
units.crse_theme: Students explore redox chemistry through the lens of historical and cultural metallurgy — ancient West African iron smelting, Chinese bronze casting, and South American gold extraction. Students also examine modern electrochemistry in batteries, corrosion, and electroplating, with attention to the environmental justice implications of battery production and disposal in communities worldwide.

formative: Exit tickets on oxidation number assignments

investigations: Investigation 9: Building and Testing a Voltaic Cell

lessons.title: Oxidation, Reduction, and Oxidation Numbers
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can assign oxidation numbers to atoms in a compound, identify which species is oxidized and which is reduced in a reaction, and explain that oxidation and reduction always occur together.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever seen metal rust, tarnish, or corrode? Where was it, and what do you think caused it to change?
lessons.do_now: When iron rusts, it combines with oxygen from the air: 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3. The iron changes from Fe(0) to Fe(3+). What happened to the iron atoms? Did they gain or lose something?
materials: Iron nail and copper sulfate solution demo
Colored pencils for tracking electron transfer

engage.description: Demo: Place an iron nail in copper sulfate solution. Within minutes, the nail develops a reddish-brown coating (copper) and the blue solution fades. Ask: Iron went into the solution and copper came out. What was exchanged between them? Introduce the idea that electrons were transferred from iron to copper — this is a redox reaction.

explore.description: Students learn the oxidation number rules systematically: (1) Free elements = 0, (2) Monatomic ions = charge, (3) Oxygen = -2 (usually), (4) Hydrogen = +1 (usually), (5) Sum of oxidation numbers = charge of species. Using these rules, students assign oxidation numbers to every atom in 10 compounds and ions. Then they examine 5 chemical equations, track changes in oxidation numbers, and identify which atoms were oxidized (increased) and which were reduced (decreased).

explain.description: Teacher formalizes definitions: Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number). Reduction = gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). Mnemonic: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). The species that is oxidized is the reducing agent (it causes reduction in the other species). The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent. Students apply these terms to the iron-copper reaction from the demo.

elaborate.description: Students analyze three more redox reactions: (1) Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (metal dissolving in acid), (2) 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO (combustion of magnesium), (3) Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag (single replacement). For each, they assign oxidation numbers, identify what is oxidized and reduced, name the oxidizing and reducing agents, and write the electron transfer.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: In the reaction 2Al + 3CuSO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3Cu: (1) Assign oxidation numbers to Al and Cu on both sides. (2) Which element is oxidized? Which is reduced? (3) Identify the oxidizing agent and reducing agent. (4) How many electrons are transferred per aluminum atom?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded oxidation number assignment guide with each rule on a separate card; include a step-by-step tracking template: 'Element ___ went from oxidation number ___ to ___, so it was ___ (oxidized/reduced).'
differentiation.on_level: Complete oxidation number assignments and redox identification as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Identify redox reactions that are not obvious single replacement reactions — such as combustion, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration — and explain the electron transfers occurring in these complex systems.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual OIL RIG mnemonic card with visual electron transfer diagrams; color-code oxidation (red, losing electrons) and reduction (blue, gaining electrons) throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice reactions from five to three; provide pre-assigned oxidation numbers for some atoms in the elaborate section; allow use of reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the ancient origins of metallurgy as redox chemistry: West African iron smelting (Haya people of Tanzania, ~2000 years ago, produced carbon steel by reducing iron ore in specially designed furnaces), Chinese bronze age technology (reducing copper and tin ores), and South American civilizations' gold and silver work. These practices represent sophisticated understanding of redox chemistry centuries before the concept was formalized by European scientists.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'oxidation': Iron is oxidized in the rusting process because___. Both iron and copper are metals, but iron is more reactive, so___. The oxidation number of iron increased from 0 to +3, so iron lost ___ electrons because___.

vocabulary.definition: The loss of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule, resulting in an increase in oxidation number
The gain of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule, resulting in a decrease in oxidation number
A number assigned to an atom that represents the number of electrons it has gained, lost, or shared in a compound
The substance that is oxidized in a redox reaction; it causes reduction in another species by donating electrons
The substance that is reduced in a redox reaction; it causes oxidation in another species by accepting electrons
A chemical reaction in which electrons are transferred from one species to another; oxidation and reduction always occur together

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is a Redox Reaction? — Electron Transfer
Section 2: Rules for Assigning Oxidation Numbers
Section 3: Identifying Oxidation and Reduction in Equations
Section 4: Oxidizing Agents and Reducing Agents
Section 5: OIL RIG — The Mnemonic That Saves You

cer.phenomenon: A student places a strip of copper metal into a solution of silver nitrate (AgNO3). Over 30 minutes, the copper strip becomes coated with silvery crystals, and the colorless solution gradually turns blue. The student claims that a redox reaction occurred.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student is correct — a redox reaction occurred because___.
cer.evidence_source: Assign oxidation numbers to copper and silver before and after the reaction, identify the electron transfer, and connect the color changes to the chemical change.
cer.reasoning_frame: Copper starts as Cu(0) and changes to ___ in solution (oxidation number ___), meaning it was___. Silver starts as Ag+ and changes to ___ on the copper strip (oxidation number ___), meaning it was___. The blue color indicates ___ ions in solution, confirming___. Copper is the ___ agent and silver is the ___ agent.

lessons.title: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write and balance half-reactions for redox processes and use the activity series to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur spontaneously.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about competitions or rankings — sports teams, music charts, or even food rankings. What makes one thing 'more active' or 'better' than another on a list?
lessons.do_now: A student places a zinc strip in copper sulfate solution and observes a reaction. Then the student places a copper strip in zinc sulfate solution and observes NO reaction. Why does one combination react and the other does not?
materials: Activity series reference table (printed and on reference table)
Metal strip samples: Zn, Cu, Mg, Fe, Pb (small pieces)
Solution set: ZnSO4, CuSO4, MgSO4, FeSO4, Pb(NO3)2 (in well plates)
Safety goggles and gloves (1 per student)

engage.description: Show a video of sodium reacting violently with water (very active metal) and gold sitting unchanged in acid (very inactive metal). Ask: What makes some metals more 'eager' to give up electrons than others? Is there a ranking? Introduce the activity series as a ranking of metals by their tendency to be oxidized.

explore.description: Micro-scale lab: Using well plates, students test combinations of metals and solutions to build their own activity series. They place small pieces of Zn, Cu, Mg, and Fe into solutions of CuSO4, ZnSO4, MgSO4, and FeSO4. For each combination, they record whether a reaction occurs (evidence: color change, metal depositing). From the pattern of which metals displace others, they rank the metals from most to least active.

explain.description: Teacher connects the results to the activity series on the reference table. Rule: A more active metal will replace a less active metal from solution. Students learn to write half-reactions: Oxidation half-reaction (metal loses electrons, e.g., Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-) and Reduction half-reaction (ion gains electrons, e.g., Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu). The overall reaction is the sum of the two half-reactions with electrons canceling.

elaborate.description: Prediction practice: Students use the activity series to predict whether 8 proposed reactions will occur. For those that will occur, they write balanced half-reactions and the overall equation. Key application: Can iron displace hydrogen from HCl? (Yes — Fe is above H on the activity series.) Can copper? (No — Cu is below H.)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions for Mg + FeCl2 -> MgCl2 + Fe. (2) Will a reaction occur if copper metal is placed in aluminum sulfate solution? Use the activity series to justify. (3) A jeweler wants to plate a ring with gold. Should the ring be the anode or cathode? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a half-reaction writing template: 'Oxidation: ___ -> ___^_+ + ___e-. Reduction: ___^_+ + ___e- -> ___.' Include an activity series with a 'more active' arrow and a highlighted rule.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the micro-scale activity series lab and prediction practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the thermite reaction (Al + Fe2O3) and explain why aluminum can reduce iron oxide, calculate the energy released, and describe a real-world application (railroad welding).
differentiation.ell: Provide visual activity series with color-coded metals and arrows showing electron transfer direction; bilingual prediction sentence frames; labeled diagram of half-reactions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce prediction problems from 8 to 5; provide activity series with highlighted sections for each problem; partner for lab work; allow reference table during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the history of bronze and iron ages as revolutions in human technology driven by understanding which metals could replace others from their ores. The Haya people of Tanzania developed advanced iron smelting techniques around 2,000 years ago that achieved temperatures rivaling modern blast furnaces. Also discuss how the activity series explains why gold and platinum are found as free metals in nature (they are the least active) while alkali metals are never found free — connecting to the economics and colonialism of gold mining.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'The activity series, a list of metals ranked by their tendency to lose electrons and undergo oxidation, allows us to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur spontaneously.' 'Zinc, a more active metal than copper, spontaneously displaces copper ions from solution because it has a greater tendency to be oxidized.'

vocabulary.definition: An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction separately, including the electrons transferred
A list of metals ranked in order of decreasing tendency to be oxidized (lose electrons)
A reaction that occurs naturally without continuous external energy input once initiated
A reaction in which a more active element replaces a less active element from a compound

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Writing Oxidation and Reduction Half-Reactions
Section 2: Balancing Half-Reactions — Electrons Must Cancel
Section 3: The Activity Series — Ranking Metals by Reactivity
Section 4: Predicting Spontaneous Reactions Using the Activity Series

cer.phenomenon: A student's silver ring tarnishes (turns black) when exposed to air containing traces of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) gas. The tarnish is silver sulfide (Ag2S). The student tries to clean the ring by soaking it in aluminum foil and baking soda solution. The tarnish disappears and the ring is shiny again.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the aluminum foil cleaned the silver ring because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to explain why aluminum can reduce silver sulfide back to silver metal, and write the half-reactions.
cer.reasoning_frame: Aluminum is ___ active than silver on the activity series, meaning it has a greater tendency to___. In this reaction, aluminum is ___ (loses electrons) and silver ions in Ag2S are ___ (gain electrons). The half-reactions are: Oxidation: ___. Reduction: ___. This works because aluminum ___ silver on the activity series.

lessons.title: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can diagram and explain how a voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy, identifying the anode, cathode, salt bridge, and direction of electron flow.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about all the batteries you use in a day — phone, laptop, remote control. Have you ever wondered how a battery actually produces electricity from chemicals inside?
lessons.do_now: A lemon battery can light a small LED. The setup uses a zinc nail and a copper penny stuck into a lemon. Which metal do you think loses electrons (anode) and which gains them (cathode)? Use the activity series to predict.
materials: Voltaic cell construction kit per group: Zn and Cu electrode strips, ZnSO4 and CuSO4 solutions, salt bridge (KNO3 in agar or filter paper soaked in KNO3), beakers, wires, voltmeter
LED bulbs or small motors (1 per group)

engage.description: Build a lemon battery in front of the class: insert a zinc nail and copper penny into a lemon, connect wires to a voltmeter. Students see a voltage reading. Ask: The lemon is not plugged into a wall outlet — where is the electrical energy coming from? The chemical reaction between zinc and the acid in the lemon produces electrons that flow through the wire. This is an electrochemical cell.

explore.description: Lab: Each group constructs a Zn/Cu voltaic cell. They set up two beakers — one with Zn in ZnSO4, one with Cu in CuSO4 — connected by a salt bridge and external wire to a voltmeter. Students record the voltage, then connect an LED or small motor. They observe which electrode gets smaller over time (anode, Zn) and which gets larger (cathode, Cu). They draw and label a complete diagram of their cell.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes voltaic cell anatomy: (1) Anode — oxidation occurs, more active metal, negative terminal, gets smaller. (2) Cathode — reduction occurs, less active metal, positive terminal, gets larger. (3) Salt bridge — allows ion flow to maintain electrical neutrality. (4) External wire — electrons flow from anode to cathode (from Zn to Cu). Students write the half-reactions and label all components on their diagram.

elaborate.description: Application: Students examine the chemistry of common batteries. For a lithium-ion battery (used in phones), they identify the half-reactions from the sample cluster (Li -> Li+ + e- at the anode; CoO2 + Li+ + e- -> LiCoO2 at the cathode). They compare voltaic cells (spontaneous, produce electricity) to the concept of electrolytic cells (non-spontaneous, use electricity — to be covered next lesson).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: A voltaic cell uses Mg and Ag electrodes. (1) Which metal is the anode? Use the activity series. (2) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions. (3) Draw an arrow showing the direction of electron flow through the external wire. (4) What is the purpose of the salt bridge?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-labeled voltaic cell diagram with blanks only for the half-reaction equations and direction of electron flow; include a 'Voltaic Cell Checklist' matching each component to its function.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the voltaic cell construction, diagram, and analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the cell potential (voltage) using standard reduction potentials from a reference table; compare predicted voltage to measured voltage and explain sources of discrepancy.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual voltaic cell diagram with all components labeled in English and native language; use arrows and color-coding (red for oxidation at anode, blue for reduction at cathode) consistently.
differentiation.iep: Partner for cell construction; provide pre-drawn cell diagram to label rather than drawing from scratch; reduce exit ticket to three parts; allow reference table use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Alessandro Volta's invention of the voltaic pile (1800), the first true battery, and how it led to the electrical age. Connect to modern battery technology and the work of John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino, who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for developing the lithium-ion battery. Discuss environmental justice issues in lithium and cobalt mining — cobalt is often mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo under dangerous conditions, including child labor, raising ethical questions about our reliance on battery-powered devices.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'voltaic cell': Zinc is the anode in a Zn/Cu voltaic cell because___. Electrons flow through the external wire from zinc to copper, but ions flow through the salt bridge in the opposite direction because___. The salt bridge is essential, so without it___.

vocabulary.definition: An electrochemical cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction
The electrode where oxidation occurs; in a voltaic cell, it is the negative terminal
The electrode where reduction occurs; in a voltaic cell, it is the positive terminal
A device containing a salt solution that allows ions to flow between the two half-cells, maintaining electrical neutrality
A conductor (usually a metal) through which electrons enter or leave an electrochemical cell
The difference in electrical potential between the anode and cathode, measured in volts; drives the flow of electrons

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is a Voltaic Cell?
Section 2: Anatomy — Anode, Cathode, Salt Bridge, External Wire
Section 3: Writing Half-Reactions for Voltaic Cells
Section 4: Direction of Electron Flow and Ion Flow
Section 5: Real-World Batteries — From Volta to Lithium-Ion

cer.phenomenon: A student builds a voltaic cell using iron and silver electrodes with appropriate salt solutions. The voltmeter reads 1.24 V. When the student removes the salt bridge, the voltage immediately drops to 0 V. The student replaces the salt bridge and the voltage returns.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the salt bridge is essential for the voltaic cell to function because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the voltage data with and without the salt bridge, and explain what happens to charge balance in each half-cell when the bridge is removed.
cer.reasoning_frame: When the cell operates, electrons flow from ___ to ___ through the wire. This causes the anode half-cell to become ___ charged (loss of negative electrons) and the cathode half-cell to become ___ charged (gain of negative electrons). Without the salt bridge, this charge buildup ___ the flow of electrons because___. The salt bridge restores balance by allowing ___ ions to migrate to the ___ half-cell and ___ ions to migrate to the ___ half-cell.

lessons.title: Electrolytic Cells and Applications
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can compare and contrast voltaic and electrolytic cells and explain how electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about something that does not happen on its own but CAN happen if you put energy into it — like pushing a car uphill. What energy source makes it possible?
lessons.do_now: In a voltaic cell, a spontaneous reaction produces electricity. What if we wanted to force a non-spontaneous reaction to happen — like separating water into hydrogen and oxygen? What would we need to provide?
materials: Electrolysis of water demo: Hoffman apparatus or simple setup with 9V battery, two graphite electrodes, water with Na2SO4 electrolyte, test tubes for gas collection
Voltaic vs. electrolytic cell comparison chart (printed)
Electroplating demo materials: copper sulfate solution, copper electrode, metal key, 6V battery

engage.description: Demo: Connect a 9V battery to two graphite electrodes in water with a small amount of Na2SO4. Students observe bubbles forming at both electrodes. Collect the gas at each electrode and test: hydrogen at the cathode (pops with a burning splint), oxygen at the anode (relights a glowing splint). Ask: We are using electricity to break water apart. Is this a spontaneous reaction? No — we had to force it with the battery.

explore.description: Comparison activity: Students receive diagram templates for both a voltaic cell and an electrolytic cell. They label both diagrams side by side, identifying: energy source (spontaneous reaction vs. external battery), direction of electron flow, anode (still oxidation) and cathode (still reduction), and sign conventions. They complete a Venn diagram highlighting similarities and differences.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: In an electrolytic cell, an external power source forces a non-spontaneous reaction to occur. The anode is still the site of oxidation and the cathode is still the site of reduction, but the sign convention is reversed (anode is positive, cathode is negative — because the battery forces electrons to the cathode). Key applications: electrolysis of water, electroplating (coating objects with metal), refining metals like aluminum (Hall-Heroult process).

elaborate.description: Electroplating demo: Teacher electroplates a metal key with copper using CuSO4 solution and a copper electrode connected to a battery. Students observe the key turning copper-colored. They identify the anode (copper electrode, being oxidized to replace Cu2+ in solution) and cathode (the key, where Cu2+ is reduced to solid copper). Students write the half-reactions and explain why the copper electrode gets smaller.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Complete a comparison table for voltaic vs. electrolytic cells (energy conversion, spontaneity, anode sign, cathode sign, example). Then: A company electroplates silver onto jewelry. (1) Should the jewelry be the anode or cathode? (2) What should the other electrode be made of? (3) Write the reduction half-reaction at the cathode.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled comparison table with half the cells completed; include a visual side-by-side diagram of both cell types with matching color-coding for anode/cathode.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the comparison activity, Venn diagram, and electroplating analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the mass of copper deposited during electroplating given current, time, and Faraday's constant. Connect electrolysis to industrial aluminum production and calculate the electrical energy cost.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual comparison chart with visual cell diagrams; sentence frames for describing differences: 'In a voltaic cell, the anode is ___, but in an electrolytic cell, the anode is ___ because___.'
differentiation.iep: Provide completed Venn diagram with one additional comparison for student to add; reduce exit ticket to comparison table only; allow partner work.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Hall-Heroult process for producing aluminum by electrolysis, developed independently by Charles Martin Hall (American) and Paul Heroult (French) in 1886. Before this process, aluminum was more expensive than gold. Highlight that Hall, an African American inventor, faced racial discrimination but persisted and revolutionized the aluminum industry. Also discuss the environmental impact of aluminum smelting, which requires enormous amounts of electricity — often generated by hydroelectric dams that displace indigenous communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'electrolysis': Water does not spontaneously decompose into hydrogen and oxygen because___. Both voltaic and electrolytic cells involve redox reactions, but they differ in energy conversion because___. The battery forces electrons to flow in the non-spontaneous direction, so___.

vocabulary.definition: An electrochemical cell that uses electrical energy from an external source to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction
The process of using electrical energy to cause a non-spontaneous chemical reaction, such as decomposing water into hydrogen and oxygen
The process of depositing a thin layer of metal onto an object by making it the cathode in an electrolytic cell
A reaction that does not occur on its own and requires continuous input of energy to proceed
A battery or power supply that provides the electrical energy needed to drive electrolysis

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Electrolytic Cells — Forcing Non-Spontaneous Reactions
Section 2: Voltaic vs. Electrolytic — Side-by-Side Comparison
Section 3: Electrolysis of Water — Decomposition with Electricity
Section 4: Electroplating — Industrial Applications
Section 5: The Hall-Heroult Process — Producing Aluminum

cer.phenomenon: A rechargeable lithium-ion battery in a smartphone operates as a voltaic cell when powering the phone (discharging) and as an electrolytic cell when plugged into a charger (charging). A student asks: 'How can the same battery be both types of cell?'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that a rechargeable battery functions as both a voltaic cell and an electrolytic cell because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the direction of electron flow and the energy conversion during discharging vs. charging, identifying which is spontaneous and which requires external energy.
cer.reasoning_frame: When the battery is discharging, the redox reaction is ___ and chemical energy is converted to___. The anode is ___ and the cathode is___. When plugged into a charger, an external power source forces electrons in the ___ direction, reversing the reaction. This is now an ___ cell because___. The products of the discharge reaction become the ___ for the charging reaction.

lessons.title: Redox and Electrochemistry Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can integrate oxidation numbers, half-reactions, activity series predictions, and electrochemical cell analysis to solve multi-step redox problems.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could prevent one metal object in your life from corroding or rusting, what would it be and why?
lessons.do_now: A voltaic cell is built using Mg and Cu electrodes. Without looking at your notes: (1) Which is the anode? (2) Which direction do electrons flow? (3) Write the two half-reactions. (4) What voltage would you expect — higher or lower than a Zn/Cu cell?
materials: Redox scenario cards (set of 10 for group activity)

engage.description: Corrosion challenge: Show images of corroded objects — a rusted bridge, a tarnished silver trophy, a green copper dome, a corroded car battery terminal. For each, students identify: What was oxidized? What was the oxidizing agent? How could the corrosion be prevented? (galvanizing, painting, sacrificial anode, electroplating).

explore.description: Scenario card activity: Groups receive redox scenario cards requiring integration of multiple concepts. Example: 'Design a voltaic cell that could protect an iron pipe from rusting. Choose an appropriate sacrificial anode using the activity series. Draw the cell, write half-reactions, and explain how cathodic protection works.' Groups present their solutions.

explain.description: Class synthesis: Build a comprehensive concept map connecting oxidation numbers, half-reactions, activity series, voltaic cells, electrolytic cells, and real-world applications. Teacher addresses common misconceptions: (1) Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. (2) The anode is not always negative — it depends on the cell type. (3) Electrons flow through the wire, but ions flow through the solution.

elaborate.description: Multi-step practice: Three cumulative problems covering the full range of unit content. Example: Given a reaction, assign oxidation numbers, write half-reactions, predict spontaneity using the activity series, and design an electrochemical cell to carry out the reaction.

evaluate.description: Unit 9 formative assessment: Five questions covering oxidation number assignment, half-reaction writing, activity series prediction, voltaic cell diagram interpretation, and voltaic vs. electrolytic cell comparison.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a unit summary reference sheet with key definitions, rules, and labeled cell diagrams; include a step-by-step problem-solving template for redox analysis.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the scenario card activity and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on one advanced application of electrochemistry: fuel cells (hydrogen fuel cell vehicles), corrosion engineering, or electrochemical sensors in medicine.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual unit summary sheet; visual concept map with labeled diagrams; allow oral presentation of scenario card solutions with written half-reactions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to three questions; provide all reference materials during assessment; partner support during scenario activity; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss corrosion prevention as a global engineering challenge. Highlight the contributions of Elijah McCoy, an African American inventor whose lubrication innovations prevented oxidation-related damage in steam engines (the phrase 'the real McCoy' is attributed to the quality of his inventions). Connect to modern corrosion engineering — the Statue of Liberty restoration in the 1980s required understanding of galvanic corrosion between its copper skin and iron framework.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Electrons transfer.' Students expand: 'In every redox reaction, electrons transfer from the reducing agent, which undergoes oxidation and loses electrons, to the oxidizing agent, which undergoes reduction and gains electrons, and this transfer of electrons can be harnessed in an electrochemical cell to produce electrical energy or can be forced by an external power source in electrolysis.'

vocabulary.definition: Corrosion that occurs when two different metals are in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte; the more active metal corrodes preferentially
A more active metal attached to a less active metal structure to preferentially corrode and protect the structure from oxidation
A corrosion prevention technique where a more active metal is used as a sacrificial anode to protect a less active metal
The branch of chemistry that studies the relationship between electrical energy and chemical reactions

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Connecting Redox Concepts — From Oxidation Numbers to Cells
Section 2: Review — Half-Reactions and the Activity Series
Section 3: Review — Voltaic vs. Electrolytic Cells
Section 4: Corrosion Prevention and Real-World Applications

cer.phenomenon: An underground steel pipeline carries natural gas. To prevent rusting, engineers attach zinc blocks to the outside of the pipe at regular intervals. Over time, the zinc blocks dissolve away but the steel pipe remains intact. The company must replace the zinc blocks every few years.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the zinc blocks protect the steel pipe through cathodic protection because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to explain why zinc corrodes instead of iron, write the relevant half-reactions, and explain the electron flow.
cer.reasoning_frame: Zinc is ___ active than iron on the activity series, meaning it has a greater tendency to___. When connected, zinc acts as the ___ (site of oxidation), donating electrons to the iron pipe. The iron becomes the ___ (site of reduction), receiving electrons. As long as zinc is present, the iron ___ because___. This is called ___ protection.

units.title: Waves, EM Radiation & Nuclear Chemistry
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Hospitals use X-rays to see bones, UV light to sterilize equipment, and radioactive isotopes to treat cancer. All of these involve electromagnetic radiation or nuclear reactions, yet some are harmless and others can be deadly. What determines whether radiation is safe or dangerous?
essential_questions: How are wavelength, frequency, and energy related in electromagnetic radiation?
How do different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation interact with matter in different ways?
What happens to the nucleus during radioactive decay, fission, and fusion, and how are these processes different from chemical reactions?
units.crse_theme: Students explore the intersection of nuclear chemistry and society — from Marie Curie's pioneering research on radioactivity (facing gender discrimination) to the devastating effects of nuclear testing on Pacific Islander and Indigenous communities (Marshall Islands, Nevada Test Site). Students also examine how radiation is used in medicine and food preservation across cultures.

summative: Unit 10 Exam: Waves, EM Radiation & Nuclear Chemistry

investigations: Investigation 10: Modeling Nuclear Decay — Half-Life Simulation with Pennies

lessons.title: Wave Properties and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can describe waves in terms of wavelength, frequency, and amplitude, and explain how electromagnetic radiation is organized by frequency and energy in the EM spectrum.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is something invisible that you interact with every day — Wi-Fi, radio signals, sunlight you cannot see? How do you know it is there if you cannot see it?
lessons.do_now: Your phone receives calls, texts, and video — all wirelessly. Your microwave heats food without touching it. A remote control changes the TV channel from across the room. What do all of these have in common?
materials: Slinky or wave demonstration spring (1 per group)
Colored pencils for labeling wave diagrams
Prism or diffraction grating (1 per group)

engage.description: Prism demo: Shine white light through a prism to produce a visible spectrum on the wall. Ask: White light looks like one thing, but it is actually made of many colors. What separates them? Each color has a different wavelength. But the visible spectrum is just a tiny slice of all electromagnetic radiation. What else is out there beyond what we can see?

explore.description: Wave modeling with slinkies: In pairs, students create transverse waves with a slinky on the floor. They experiment with: (1) making waves with long vs. short wavelengths, (2) making waves with high vs. low frequency (fast vs. slow shaking), (3) making waves with large vs. small amplitude. They observe the inverse relationship between wavelength and frequency (shorter wavelength = faster frequency). They sketch and label three waves: high frequency/short wavelength, low frequency/long wavelength, and high amplitude.

explain.description: Teacher introduces key relationships: c = wavelength x frequency (where c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s). As frequency increases, wavelength decreases. Energy of a photon: E = hf (where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J-s). Higher frequency = higher energy. Students label the EM spectrum from lowest to highest energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray. They calculate wavelength and energy for sample frequencies.

elaborate.description: Application: Students match EM radiation types to real-world uses and explain why each type is suited for that use: radio waves for communication (low energy, passes through walls), microwaves for cooking (absorbed by water molecules), infrared for thermal imaging (emitted by warm objects), UV for sterilization (high enough energy to damage DNA), X-rays for medical imaging (passes through soft tissue, absorbed by bone).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the frequency of light with a wavelength of 5.0 x 10^-7 m. (2) Calculate the energy of a photon with frequency 6.0 x 10^14 Hz. (3) Which has more energy — a radio wave or an X-ray? Explain using the relationship E = hf.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a labeled EM spectrum with frequency and energy arrows already drawn; include a step-by-step calculation template for c = wavelength x frequency and E = hf with units labeled.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the wave modeling, EM spectrum analysis, and calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the wavelength of electrons using the de Broglie equation and compare to electromagnetic radiation wavelengths, connecting to the wave-particle duality of matter.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual EM spectrum reference card with visual icons for each type of radiation and its uses; formula cards with variable definitions in both languages.
differentiation.iep: Pre-drawn wave diagrams for labeling instead of sketching from scratch; allow calculator for all problems; reduce calculation problems from three to two; enlarged formula reference.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how different cultures have understood and used electromagnetic radiation throughout history: ancient use of fire (infrared radiation) for warmth and cooking, Arabic scholars' contributions to optics (Ibn al-Haytham's 11th-century work on light, considered the father of modern optics), and the development of radio communication by Guglielmo Marconi and Jagadish Chandra Bose (whose contributions as an Indian physicist were initially overlooked). Also discuss how communities near cell towers have raised concerns about EM radiation exposure — an ongoing public health and environmental justice discussion.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'electromagnetic radiation': X-rays have more energy than radio waves because___. Visible light and gamma rays are both electromagnetic radiation, but gamma rays are far more dangerous because___. The speed of all EM radiation is the same (c), so if wavelength decreases, frequency must___.

vocabulary.definition: The distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs of a wave, measured in meters (m) or nanometers (nm)
The number of wave cycles that pass a given point per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
The maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position; related to the wave's intensity or brightness
The full range of electromagnetic radiation organized by frequency and wavelength, from radio waves to gamma rays
A discrete packet of electromagnetic energy; the energy of a photon is determined by its frequency (E = hf)
The speed at which all electromagnetic radiation travels in a vacuum: 3.0 x 10^8 m/s

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Wave Properties — Wavelength, Frequency, Amplitude
Section 2: The Wave Equation: c = wavelength x frequency
Section 3: The Electromagnetic Spectrum — From Radio to Gamma
Section 4: Photon Energy: E = hf
Section 5: EM Radiation in Everyday Life

cer.phenomenon: Sunscreen labels say they protect against UV-A and UV-B radiation but not visible light. Dermatologists warn that UV radiation causes skin cancer, but visible light from the same sun does not. Both are electromagnetic radiation from the same source.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that UV radiation is more harmful than visible light because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the relationship E = hf and the position of UV and visible light on the EM spectrum to compare their energies.
cer.reasoning_frame: UV radiation has a ___ frequency than visible light, which means each UV photon carries ___ energy (E = hf). This higher energy is sufficient to ___ the bonds in DNA molecules in skin cells, while visible light photons have ___ energy and cannot___. This is why___ radiation causes cancer while ___ light does not.

lessons.title: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation interact with matter through absorption, transmission, and reflection, and evaluate claims about the effects of EM radiation.
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever gotten a sunburn? What was happening to your skin at the atomic level that made it red and painful?
lessons.do_now: A greenhouse stays warm because glass transmits visible light but absorbs infrared radiation. How does this relate to climate change and the greenhouse effect?
materials: Various materials for testing: glass, plastic wrap, sunscreen, fabric, sunglasses
UV flashlight or access to sunlight
Published claims about EM radiation (3 articles, printed excerpts)

engage.description: UV bead activity: Give each student a few UV-sensitive beads. Indoors, they are white. Take them near a window or use a UV flashlight — they change color instantly. Ask: What type of radiation caused this change? Then test: Does the color change happen through glass? Through sunscreen? Through fabric? Students record which materials block UV and which transmit it.

explore.description: Testing materials: Groups systematically test which materials transmit, absorb, or reflect UV radiation using the beads as detectors. They test: clear glass, sunglasses, plastic wrap, aluminum foil, sunscreen (SPF 15 vs. SPF 50), different colors of fabric, and water. They organize results in a data table. They also read two short published claims about EM radiation effects (e.g., 'Cell phones cause cancer' and 'UV water purification is safe for drinking').

explain.description: Teacher explains three wave-matter interactions: (1) Absorption — material absorbs the radiation's energy (UV absorbed by sunscreen, infrared absorbed by greenhouse gases). (2) Transmission — radiation passes through (visible light through glass). (3) Reflection — radiation bounces off (visible light off a mirror, radio waves off the ionosphere). The interaction depends on the frequency of the radiation and the molecular structure of the material.

elaborate.description: Claim evaluation: Students evaluate the two published claims from the Explore phase using scientific evidence. They assess: Is the claim supported by evidence about EM radiation frequency, energy, and interaction with matter? They write a paragraph evaluating each claim's validity, citing specific evidence about photon energy and molecular interactions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Explain why greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation but not visible light (hint: molecular vibration frequencies). (2) A company claims their product 'blocks all harmful radiation.' Evaluate this claim — what types of radiation are harmful, and what would the product need to do? (3) Why does higher SPF sunscreen provide more UV protection?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a graphic organizer with three columns: Absorption, Transmission, Reflection — students sort examples into columns; include sentence frames for claim evaluation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the UV bead investigation and claim evaluation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how spectroscopy uses absorption patterns to identify unknown substances and explain how astronomers determine the composition of distant stars using absorption spectra.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual diagrams of absorption, transmission, and reflection with bilingual labels; simplified article excerpts with key vocabulary highlighted; sentence frames for evaluation paragraphs.
differentiation.iep: Reduce claim evaluation to one article instead of two; provide a claim evaluation scaffold with guiding questions; partner for UV bead investigation; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the greenhouse effect and climate change as a global environmental justice issue — rising sea levels disproportionately threaten Pacific Island nations and coastal communities in the Global South, while industrial nations produce the most greenhouse gas emissions. Also discuss how UV water purification technology (SODIS — Solar Water Disinfection) has been deployed in developing countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America to provide safe drinking water using only sunlight and plastic bottles — an application of understanding how UV radiation interacts with biological matter.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'absorption': Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere because they absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface. Visible light passes through the atmosphere, but infrared radiation is absorbed by CO2 and methane, so___. Sunscreen absorbs UV radiation, so the photons' energy is converted to ___ instead of damaging___.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which matter takes in electromagnetic radiation energy, often converting it to thermal energy or causing electronic transitions
The process by which electromagnetic radiation passes through matter without being absorbed
The process by which electromagnetic radiation bounces off a surface
Electromagnetic radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, including UV, X-rays, and gamma rays
Electromagnetic radiation without enough energy to ionize atoms, including radio waves, microwaves, infrared, and visible light

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Three Types of Wave-Matter Interactions
Section 2: Absorption — How Materials Capture Radiation Energy
Section 3: The Greenhouse Effect — Infrared Absorption by Gases
Section 4: Evaluating Claims About EM Radiation and Health

cer.phenomenon: A company advertises a sticker that claims to 'block harmful cell phone radiation and protect your brain.' The sticker costs $30 and contains a thin copper layer. Cell phones emit radio waves with frequencies around 800-2000 MHz.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that this product's claim is ___ (valid/not scientifically supported) because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use knowledge of EM radiation types, photon energy at cell phone frequencies, and the difference between ionizing and non-ionizing radiation to evaluate the claim.
cer.reasoning_frame: Cell phones emit ___ waves, which are classified as ___ radiation because their photon energy (E = hf = ___) is ___ than the energy needed to ionize atoms or break chemical bonds. The scientific consensus is that ___. Even if the copper sticker blocked some radiation, it would also ___ the phone's signal, which means___.

lessons.title: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can write balanced nuclear equations for alpha decay, beta decay, and positron emission, and compare fission, fusion, and radioactive decay in terms of changes to the nucleus and energy released.
lessons.circle_prompt: The Sun has been shining for about 4.6 billion years. Where does all that energy come from? It is not burning like a campfire — so what is different?
lessons.do_now: In a chemical reaction like 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, the atoms rearrange but no atoms are created or destroyed. In a nuclear reaction, one element can change into a completely different element. How is this possible?
materials: Nuclear decay simulation cards (alpha, beta, positron — 1 set per group)
Nuclear fission and fusion diagram handout (printed)
Pennies for half-life simulation (30 per student)

engage.description: Show a dramatic video comparing a chemical explosion (TNT) with a nuclear explosion (atomic bomb test footage, historically contextualized). The nuclear explosion releases millions of times more energy from the same mass of material. Ask: Chemical reactions rearrange electrons. What is different about the nuclear reaction that produces so much more energy? The answer: nuclear reactions change the nucleus itself, converting tiny amounts of mass into enormous amounts of energy.

explore.description: Card-based nuclear decay modeling: Students use cards representing protons, neutrons, and nuclear particles to model three types of decay. (1) Alpha decay: remove a card with 2 protons + 2 neutrons (He-4 nucleus) from a uranium-238 nucleus and determine the daughter isotope. (2) Beta decay: convert a neutron card to a proton card plus an electron, modeling C-14 decay. (3) Positron emission: convert a proton to a neutron plus a positron. For each, students write the nuclear equation and verify that mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes: In nuclear reactions, the nucleus changes composition. Alpha decay: nucleus emits He-4, atomic number decreases by 2, mass number by 4. Beta decay: neutron becomes proton + electron, atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged. Fission: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and energy (used in nuclear power plants). Fusion: light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus plus energy (powers the Sun). All nuclear reactions obey conservation of mass number and atomic number. E = mc^2 explains the enormous energy: tiny mass loss converts to huge energy.

elaborate.description: Half-life simulation: Each student starts with 30 pennies (representing radioactive atoms). They shake and flip all pennies, remove those showing tails (decayed), record the number remaining, and repeat for 6 rounds. They graph the number of remaining atoms vs. number of half-lives and observe the exponential decay curve. Teacher connects to real-world half-lives: C-14 (5,730 years, used in carbon dating), I-131 (8 days, used in thyroid treatment), U-238 (4.5 billion years, used in geological dating).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of Ra-226. (2) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the beta decay of Co-60. (3) Compare fission and fusion: Which splits atoms? Which combines them? Which powers the Sun? Which powers nuclear reactors?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a nuclear equation balancing template: '___ -> ___ + ___. Check: mass numbers add up? Atomic numbers add up?' Include a reference card showing the particles (alpha = He-4, beta = electron, positron, neutron) with their mass and atomic numbers.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the card modeling, half-life simulation, and nuclear equation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the energy released in a specific nuclear reaction using E = mc^2 and the mass defect between reactants and products. Compare to energy released in a chemical reaction.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual nuclear particle reference card with symbols and visual representations; color-coded nuclear equations (protons in red, neutrons in blue, emitted particles in green); sentence frames for comparing fission and fusion.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted nuclear equation templates with blanks for missing values; reduce balancing problems from five to three; partner for half-life simulation; allow reference cards during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Marie Curie's groundbreaking research on radioactivity — she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry). Despite her genius, she faced significant gender discrimination. Also discuss the devastating impacts of nuclear testing on indigenous and Pacific Islander communities: the Marshall Islands (Castle Bravo test, 1954), the Navajo Nation (uranium mining leaving contaminated land and elevated cancer rates), and the environmental justice movement demanding cleanup and reparations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'nuclear decay': Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay because___. Both fission and fusion release enormous amounts of energy, but they are opposite processes because___. The half-life of C-14 is 5,730 years, so after 11,460 years, only ___ of the original C-14 remains because___.

vocabulary.definition: The spontaneous emission of radiation (alpha, beta, or gamma) from an unstable nucleus to become more stable
A type of nuclear decay in which the nucleus emits an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons, equivalent to a He-4 nucleus)
A type of nuclear decay in which a neutron converts to a proton and emits a beta particle (high-speed electron)
A nuclear reaction in which a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing neutrons and a large amount of energy
A nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing enormous energy (powers the Sun)
The time required for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay
Einstein's equation showing that mass can be converted to energy; the small mass loss in nuclear reactions produces enormous energy

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Chemical Reactions vs. Nuclear Reactions
Section 2: Types of Radioactive Decay — Alpha, Beta, Gamma
Section 3: Writing and Balancing Nuclear Equations
Section 4: Fission and Fusion — Splitting and Combining Nuclei
Section 5: Half-Life and Radioactive Dating

cer.phenomenon: The Sun fuses approximately 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second. Yet the Sun has been shining for 4.6 billion years and still has enough hydrogen to last billions more. In contrast, a coal-fired power plant burns through millions of tons of coal per year to produce far less energy.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that nuclear fusion produces vastly more energy per unit mass than chemical combustion because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the energy source in nuclear fusion (mass-energy conversion via E=mc^2) with the energy source in combustion (bond energy changes), and use the given data about the Sun's fuel consumption.
cer.reasoning_frame: In chemical combustion, energy comes from ___, which involves rearranging___. In nuclear fusion, energy comes from ___, which involves converting a small amount of ___ into energy according to E=mc^2. Because c^2 = ___, even a tiny mass loss produces ___ energy. This explains why the Sun, despite consuming ___ tons of hydrogen per second, can sustain fusion for billions of years.

lessons.title: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can evaluate the benefits and risks of nuclear technology applications and demonstrate mastery of wave properties, EM radiation, and nuclear chemistry concepts.
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could use nuclear technology to solve one problem in the world — energy, medicine, food safety, or something else — what would you choose and why?
lessons.do_now: A patient receives a dose of radioactive iodine-131 (half-life = 8 days) for thyroid cancer treatment. After 24 days, what fraction of the original dose remains in the patient's body? Show your work.
materials: Nuclear applications reading set (4 short articles: nuclear medicine, nuclear power, food irradiation, carbon dating)

engage.description: Four corners activity: Post four signs around the room: Nuclear Power, Nuclear Medicine, Food Irradiation, Nuclear Weapons. Students move to the topic they think is most important for society to understand. Each group shares one reason for their choice. Teacher frames the discussion: nuclear technology has tremendous benefits and serious risks — understanding the science helps us make informed decisions.

explore.description: Jigsaw reading: Each group reads one short article about a nuclear application. Group A: Nuclear medicine (PET scans, radiation therapy using targeted isotopes). Group B: Nuclear power (fission reactors, waste storage challenges). Group C: Food irradiation (using gamma rays to kill bacteria, extending shelf life). Group D: Carbon dating (using C-14 half-life to determine age of artifacts). Each group completes a benefits-risks T-chart for their application.

explain.description: Groups present their application to the class. Teacher synthesizes: all nuclear applications involve the same fundamental science (radioactive decay, radiation interactions with matter) but applied in different contexts. Key distinction: the dose and type of radiation determine whether it is helpful or harmful. Students take notes from peer presentations and complete T-charts for all four applications.

elaborate.description: Cumulative review: Students work through multi-step problems integrating wave properties, EM radiation, and nuclear chemistry. Example: Calculate the energy of a gamma ray photon emitted during Co-60 decay, compare to X-ray photon energy, and explain why both are used in medical applications but require different safety precautions.

evaluate.description: Unit 10 formative assessment: Six questions covering wave calculations (c = wavelength x frequency, E = hf), EM spectrum identification, wave-matter interactions, nuclear equation balancing, half-life calculations, and fission vs. fusion comparison.

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-organized T-chart templates with one benefit and one risk already filled in for each application; include a unit formula reference sheet for all calculations.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the jigsaw reading, presentations, and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Write a persuasive essay arguing for or against expanding nuclear power in the United States, using scientific evidence about fission, waste storage, safety, and comparison to fossil fuels and renewable energy.
