differentiation.ell: Provide simplified reading excerpts with key vocabulary defined in margins; bilingual T-chart template; visual formula cards for all calculations; allow oral presentation.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide all formula references; partner support during jigsaw reading; extended time; allow T-chart completion from peer presentations rather than reading.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the environmental justice dimensions of nuclear power and waste. The Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository proposal disproportionately affected the Western Shoshone Nation. Uranium mining on Navajo Nation lands left contaminated water sources and elevated cancer rates that persist today. Contrast with the potential of nuclear power to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change — highlighting the complexity of this issue. Also discuss Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese American physicist whose experimental work on beta decay disproved the law of conservation of parity, yet her male colleagues received the Nobel Prize for the theoretical prediction.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Radiation interacts with matter.' Students expand: 'Electromagnetic radiation interacts with matter through absorption, transmission, and reflection, and the specific interaction depends on the frequency of the radiation and the molecular structure of the material, which is why high-frequency ionizing radiation like gamma rays can damage DNA while low-frequency radio waves pass harmlessly through the body.'

vocabulary.definition: The use of radioactive isotopes for diagnosis (imaging) and treatment (radiation therapy) of diseases
A method of determining the age of organic materials by measuring the ratio of C-14 to C-12 remaining in the sample
The process of exposing food to ionizing radiation (usually gamma rays) to kill bacteria, extend shelf life, and reduce spoilage
The generation of electricity using the energy released from controlled nuclear fission reactions in a reactor
Materials that remain radioactive after use in nuclear power or medicine, requiring safe long-term storage

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Nuclear Medicine — Diagnosis and Treatment
Section 2: Nuclear Power — Benefits and Waste Challenges
Section 3: Food Irradiation and Carbon Dating
Section 4: Cumulative Review — Waves, EM Radiation, and Nuclear Chemistry

cer.phenomenon: A community near a proposed nuclear power plant is divided. Supporters argue it will provide clean energy with no carbon emissions. Opponents argue the risk of meltdown and the problem of radioactive waste make it too dangerous. Both sides present data and emotional arguments.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the decision about building the nuclear plant should consider both ___ and ___ because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use scientific evidence about fission reactions, energy output, waste products, safety records, and comparison to fossil fuel emissions to evaluate both perspectives.
cer.reasoning_frame: Nuclear fission produces energy by ___, and the amount of energy per kilogram of fuel is ___ compared to fossil fuels. The main benefit is ___ because___. However, the main risks include ___ because___. A scientifically informed decision would weigh ___ against ___ and also consider___.

units.title: Engineering Design & Review
units.anchoring_phenomenon: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch contains an estimated 80,000 tons of plastic debris. Engineers and chemists are developing solutions — from biodegradable plastics to ocean cleanup devices to chemical recycling methods. How can chemistry knowledge be applied through the engineering design process to address real-world problems like plastic pollution?
essential_questions: How do engineers use the design process to develop solutions to complex real-world problems?
How does chemistry knowledge help us evaluate the trade-offs and constraints of proposed solutions?
How can we apply our understanding of all chemistry concepts to solve problems and prepare for the Regents examination?
units.crse_theme: Students apply chemistry to real-world problems that affect diverse communities — from clean water access in developing nations to green chemistry alternatives to hazardous industrial processes. Students examine how engineering solutions must account for social, cultural, and environmental impacts, especially on marginalized communities.
investigations: Investigation 11: Engineering Design Challenge — Solving a Chemistry-Based Problem

lessons.title: The Engineering Design Process
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply the engineering design process to define a problem, identify criteria and constraints, and propose a chemistry-based solution that accounts for trade-offs.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a problem in your community or school that you wish someone would solve. What would the ideal solution look like, and what limitations might make it hard to achieve?
lessons.do_now: A city's water supply contains lead from old pipes. List three possible solutions, and for each, identify one advantage and one limitation (cost, time, effectiveness, environmental impact).

dci: ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems

materials: Case study packets: 3 chemistry-based engineering challenges (printed)

engage.description: Show a short video about The Ocean Cleanup project — a real engineering effort to remove plastic from the Pacific Ocean. Ask: This seems like a simple idea (scoop up plastic), but why has it taken years of design, testing, and revision? What makes real-world engineering problems so complex? Introduce the engineering design process: Define the problem, research, brainstorm solutions, evaluate trade-offs, prototype, test, and refine.

explore.description: Case study analysis: Groups each receive a different chemistry-based engineering challenge: (A) Designing a water filtration system for a community with arsenic-contaminated groundwater, (B) Developing a biodegradable alternative to plastic packaging, (C) Creating a low-cost battery for off-grid communities. For their challenge, groups define the problem, identify criteria (what the solution must achieve) and constraints (budget, materials, time, safety, environmental impact), and brainstorm at least three possible solutions.

explain.description: Teacher formalizes the engineering design process steps and key vocabulary. Criteria = what the solution must do (effectiveness, safety, durability). Constraints = limitations on the solution (cost, available materials, time, environmental regulations). Trade-offs = accepting less of one desirable quality to gain more of another. Students learn to use a trade-off analysis matrix to systematically compare solutions against multiple criteria.

elaborate.description: Groups complete a trade-off analysis matrix for their three proposed solutions, rating each solution on a 1-5 scale for effectiveness, cost, feasibility, safety, and environmental impact. They select the best solution and prepare a 2-minute pitch explaining their choice with evidence.

evaluate.description: Gallery walk presentations: Each group presents their problem, proposed solution, and trade-off analysis. Peers provide feedback using a structured rubric: Is the problem clearly defined? Are criteria and constraints realistic? Is the trade-off analysis thorough? Is the chemistry connection clear?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed problem definition template with guiding questions: 'What is the problem? Who is affected? What science is involved?' Include a sample trade-off matrix with one row completed.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the case study analysis and trade-off matrix as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the actual engineering solutions being developed for their case study problem and compare their group's proposed solution to real-world approaches, identifying what professionals considered that students may have overlooked.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual engineering design vocabulary cards; visual flowchart of the design process; sentence frames for the presentation: 'Our problem is___. The best solution is ___ because it scores highest on___ while still meeting the constraint of___.'
differentiation.iep: Assign a specific role in the group (problem definer, criteria lister, or matrix filler); provide simplified case study with reduced reading level; allow visual presentation instead of verbal.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how engineering design must consider equity and access. The Flint, Michigan water crisis demonstrated how engineering failures disproportionately affect communities of color and low-income residents. Highlight the work of Marc Edwards, a Virginia Tech engineer who exposed the lead contamination by applying chemistry knowledge (lead solubility and corrosion chemistry), and LeeAnne Walters, a Flint resident and mother who became a citizen scientist. Connect to green chemistry principles developed by Paul Anastas and John Warner — designing chemical processes that prevent pollution rather than cleaning it up afterward.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'engineering design': The engineering design process requires defining criteria and constraints because___. The biodegradable plastic solution scored high on environmental impact, but it scored low on cost, so the team had to consider___. A solution may be scientifically effective, but if it is too expensive for the community, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A systematic approach to solving problems that includes defining the problem, researching, brainstorming solutions, evaluating trade-offs, prototyping, testing, and refining
The requirements that a successful solution must meet, such as effectiveness, safety, and durability
The limitations on a solution, including budget, available materials, time, and regulations
A compromise in which gaining one quality requires accepting less of another
A preliminary model or version of a solution built for testing and evaluation
The design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste

Section 2: Defining the Problem — Criteria and Constraints
Section 3: Brainstorming and Evaluating Solutions
Section 4: Trade-Off Analysis — Comparing Options Systematically
Section 5: Green Chemistry — Designing Safer Solutions

cer.phenomenon: A coastal city needs to build a new desalination plant to convert seawater to drinking water. Three designs are proposed: (A) Reverse osmosis (effective but uses a lot of electricity), (B) Solar-powered distillation (low energy cost but slow output), (C) Electrodialysis (moderate energy, moderate output, but expensive membranes). The city has a limited budget and a growing population.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Design ___ is the best option for this city because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the criteria (water output, energy efficiency, cost) and constraints (limited budget, growing population) to evaluate each design using a trade-off analysis.
cer.reasoning_frame: Design A excels at ___ but fails at ___ because___. Design B is strong at ___ but limited by ___ because___. Design C balances ___ and ___, making it the best compromise for a city that needs ___ while staying within___. However, this choice requires accepting the trade-off of___.

lessons.title: Applying Chemistry to Real-World Problems
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply chemistry knowledge from the entire course to analyze and propose solutions to real-world problems involving materials science, environmental remediation, or green chemistry.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is one way chemistry has already improved your life today — medicine, materials, food, technology? What is one chemistry-related problem you wish scientists would solve?
lessons.do_now: Plastic pollution is one of the biggest environmental challenges. Using your chemistry knowledge, explain why most plastics do not decompose (think about bond strength and molecular structure) and propose one chemistry-based approach to the problem.
materials: Real-world problem cards (set of 6, one per group topic)
Chemistry concept connection chart (printed — lists all major topics with space for application)
Computer simulation access or printed data for modeling (optional)
Poster paper and markers for solution presentations

engage.description: Quick challenge: Teacher names a real-world problem and students race to identify which chemistry concept is most relevant. Examples: 'Acid rain damaging buildings' (acids and bases), 'Batteries dying' (electrochemistry), 'Food spoiling' (reaction rates), 'Nuclear waste storage' (nuclear chemistry), 'Drug design' (bonding and molecular structure). This reinforces that every unit in the course connects to real-world applications.

explore.description: Design challenge: Each group selects or is assigned a real-world problem card. They must: (1) Identify the specific chemistry concepts involved (from any unit in the course), (2) Propose a solution using the engineering design process, (3) Evaluate their solution against criteria and constraints, (4) Create a poster or presentation summarizing their problem, chemistry connection, proposed solution, and trade-off analysis. Topics include: water purification, biodegradable materials, battery recycling, carbon capture, medication delivery systems, and sustainable agriculture.

explain.description: Brief teacher facilitation connecting student projects to the five Regents exam claims: Structure and Properties of Matter, Chemical Reactions, Energy, Waves and EM Radiation, and Engineering Design. Students see how their solutions integrate multiple claims.

elaborate.description: Poster presentations and peer evaluation: Groups present their solutions (2 minutes each). Peers evaluate using a rubric assessing: scientific accuracy, clear problem definition, consideration of trade-offs, and feasibility. Teacher highlights strong examples of chemistry application in each project.

evaluate.description: Written reflection: Students write a one-paragraph response answering: 'Choose one chemistry concept from this course and explain how it connects to a problem that matters to you or your community. Describe how understanding the chemistry could help solve the problem.'

differentiation.approaching: Provide a concept-to-application matching sheet listing each unit topic alongside example real-world problems; include a poster template with pre-labeled sections (Problem, Chemistry Connection, Solution, Trade-Offs).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the design challenge and poster presentation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Propose a multi-step solution that integrates chemistry concepts from at least three different units and evaluate it using quantitative criteria (calculate energy, concentrations, or costs where applicable).
differentiation.ell: Provide problem cards with simplified language and visual context images; bilingual poster template; allow bilingual presentation; sentence frames for written reflection.
differentiation.iep: Assign a focused role in the group project; provide a shortened written reflection prompt; allow visual or oral response as alternative to paragraph writing; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight diverse scientists working on real-world chemistry solutions today: James Mitchell Crow's reporting on green chemistry innovations, the work of Tessy Thomas ('Missile Woman of India') on propulsion chemistry, and community-based environmental justice organizations like WE ACT for Environmental Justice in Harlem, which uses chemistry data to advocate for clean air in their neighborhood. Discuss how students can become citizen scientists and community advocates by applying their chemistry knowledge.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'green chemistry': Green chemistry aims to prevent pollution rather than clean it up because___. A biodegradable plastic would reduce ocean pollution, but current biodegradable materials are more expensive, so researchers are working to___. Understanding bond energy helps chemists design plastics that decompose naturally because___.

vocabulary.definition: The process of removing contaminants from soil, water, or air to restore environmental quality
The interdisciplinary study of the properties and applications of materials, including metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites
Chemical practices and processes designed to meet current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
An evaluation of the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction through manufacturing, use, and disposal

cer.phenomenon: A factory discharges wastewater containing dissolved heavy metals (lead and mercury ions) into a river. Downstream communities use the river as their drinking water source. A team of chemists proposes using precipitation reactions (adding sulfide ions to form insoluble metal sulfides) to remove the heavy metals before discharge.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that using precipitation reactions is a viable method for removing heavy metals from wastewater because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use knowledge of solubility rules, precipitation reactions, and the formation of insoluble compounds to explain how PbS and HgS would form and be removed by filtration.
cer.reasoning_frame: When sulfide ions (S2-) are added to the wastewater, they react with Pb2+ to form ___ and with Hg2+ to form___, both of which are ___ according to solubility rules. These precipitates can be removed by ___, leaving the water with significantly reduced metal ion concentrations. The trade-offs of this approach include ___ and ___, but the benefit of protecting downstream communities' drinking water justifies___.

lessons.title: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can demonstrate mastery of all major chemistry concepts by analyzing multi-concept problems in the style of the Regents examination in Physical Science: Chemistry.
lessons.circle_prompt: What is the most interesting thing you learned in chemistry this year? How has it changed the way you see the world around you?

materials: Flashcard materials for student-created review tools

engage.description: Self-assessment survey: Students rate their confidence (1-5) on each major topic area from the course. Teacher tallies class results to identify the areas needing the most review. This data drives the focus of the review session.

explore.description: Regents-style practice clusters: Students work through three question clusters modeled after the Physical Science: Chemistry exam format. Each cluster includes a phenomenon-based stimulus with reading passages, data tables, and diagrams, followed by 4-5 questions (mix of multiple choice and constructed response) that span multiple performance expectations. Students work individually first, then compare answers with a partner.

explain.description: Teacher reviews the practice clusters, focusing on the most commonly missed questions. For each, teacher models the thinking process: identify the PE being tested, find the relevant information in the stimulus, apply the correct chemistry concept, and construct a complete response. Emphasize how to use the reference table effectively.

elaborate.description: Student-created review tools: Each student creates 5 flashcards for concepts they rated lowest on the self-assessment. Each card must include the concept, a definition or formula, an example or diagram, and a connection to a real-world application. Students exchange cards with a partner and quiz each other.

evaluate.description: Final reflection and goal-setting: Students complete a brief course reflection: (1) What chemistry concept was most meaningful to you and why? (2) How will you prepare for the Regents exam? (3) How might you use chemistry knowledge beyond this class? Teacher collects and provides written feedback.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a structured review guide organized by unit with key formulas, vocabulary, and one sample problem per topic; allow use of all notes and reference materials during practice clusters.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the practice clusters and flashcard creation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Create a study guide for a peer that includes practice problems, mnemonics, and concept maps connecting ideas across units. Present one topic as a 3-minute review lesson to the class.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual review guide with visual concept maps; allow reference table use in native language if available; sentence frames for constructed response questions; oral option for reflection.
differentiation.iep: Provide individualized review checklist based on prior assessment data; allow extended time for practice clusters; reduce flashcard requirement to 3; provide study guide with worked examples for each topic.

lessons.crse_connection: Final reflection on the diversity of chemists and chemistry traditions explored throughout the course — from ancient metallurgists in Africa and Asia to Marie Curie, Alice Ball, Marie Maynard Daly, Gertrude Elion, and Chien-Shiung Wu. Emphasize that chemistry is a human endeavor built by people of all backgrounds, and that students carry forward this tradition as scientifically literate citizens who can use chemistry knowledge to understand and improve their world.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So cumulative: Students write one Because/But/So sentence set connecting concepts from TWO different units. Example: 'Increasing temperature speeds up a reaction rate because it increases the kinetic energy of particles (Unit 7), but it also shifts an exothermic equilibrium toward reactants (Unit 7), so industrial chemists must find a compromise between rate and yield.'

cer.phenomenon: A new electric vehicle battery company claims their lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery is safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly than traditional lithium-cobalt-oxide batteries, though it has slightly lower energy density. The company asks: 'Is this battery the best option for widespread adoption?'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the LFP battery is/is not the best option for widespread adoption because___.
cer.evidence_source: Integrate chemistry concepts from multiple units: electrochemistry (cell design and voltage), energy (enthalpy and bond stability), materials science (element properties from the periodic table), and engineering design (trade-off analysis of criteria and constraints).
cer.reasoning_frame: From an electrochemistry perspective, the LFP battery works by___. Its lower energy density means ___, which is a limitation for___. However, iron is ___ than cobalt on the periodic table, making it more abundant and___. The engineering trade-off between energy density and ___ means that for applications like ___, the LFP battery is preferable because___. For applications requiring ___, the cobalt battery may be better because___.
